metadata.title: Water Restoration Business - Estimates (Maximize Self-Pay & Insurance Payouts)
metadata.author: Shane O'Dazier | RestorationProfits
metadata.shortDescription:
Want me to help grow your company?      Go here: www.workwithshane.com :point_left:
Want more content like this:  :point_right:  https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL932B0lp8SvL3xSjEYV-kkWJLQXJCtO34 

It is both an art and science when it comes to writing estimates for water damage.  Knowing your cost isn't enough... you have to understand the ART OF DELIVERY!

Yes, sales has made its way into the estimating process.  

If you don't understand what I am talking about... then you need to watch this video.

We explore the various gradients or thresholds that customers have and use to make buying decisions. 

Guess a number to high and they may say no.  

Guess a number too low and you lose money (boo). 

There is a sweet spot and you need to find it.

I promise you this... until you master the ART of estimating, you WILL be leaving money on the table.

There are some important variables that need to be nailed down before we can write a solid estimate.

Is this a self pay or insurance job?

Is the job large loss or is it a normal water damage under $15k

Details matter!

Want me to help you grow your restoration company?  


Go to www.WorkWithShane.com Fill out the form and let's get on a call!

metadata.author: Shane O'Dazier | RestorationProfits
metadata.shortDescription:
Want me to help you grow your company? Go here: https://www.WorkWithShane.com 👈

Want more videos like this : 👉 ✅ Getting More Restoration Jobs | Sales & ...

I've made millions with my Restoration Business. I can show you how to do the same!
---
Tired of insurance companies cutting your invoices in half and dragging out payments for months? If so, this video is for you!

Chances are, you're making critical billing mistakes that are costing your water restoration business THOUSANDS of dollars per claim.

This video reveals the biggest mistake contractors make when billing insurance...and it's not what you think! 

Here's what we'll cover:
- Why insurance companies have a legal obligation to pay as little as possible
- The critical difference between invoices vs. estimates (and why it matters)
- How to create profitable estimates that include risk factors
- Why you should never submit dry logs with your initial estimate
- Documentation mistakes that hurt your water damage restoration claims
- Strategies to avoid payment delays and get paid what you're worth

Stop letting insurance adjusters nickel and dime your restoration business! Understanding proper billing is crucial for company growth. 

If you're tired of invoices getting cut in half or waiting months to get paid, start implementing these strategies in your business today! 

-- 
WARNING - I'm not a guru or a fancy consultant.  I grew up in a trailer in Alabama and I made C's in school my entire life.  I struggled for years but eventually I found the restoration industry and I've made millions of dollars since then.  

Now I help other contractors build their version of the American Dream!  It works.

Learn how to start a water mitigation in XactScope.

Chapters

segments.text: If you are new to XactScope and do not have it set it up, check out the 'Getting
started with XactScope" video before continuing with this one.
In this video, you will learn how to get a water mitigation estimate started in XactScope.
For this example, we’ll imagine a kitchen and living room with a water loss due to a
blocked drain.
Before you begin your estimate in XactScope, is it important you already have
a completed sketch of the damaged area.
XactScope walks you through the steps to add the necessary line items to the estimate.
The first step is to add on your sketch where you intend to put any containment barriers,
essentially, creating drying chambers or divisions in the home.
To add a barrier, sketch a missing wall that surrounds the water damage in the living room.
To help you stay organized, edit the room name noting either Wet or Dry and making one
or the other a sub room.
Next, change the wall to a barrier, select the wall or multiple walls by holding the
control key, open the wall properties, and change Missing (end to end) to yes, creating
a missing wall.
Then you will want to select the mitigation barrier to Yes.
This allows you to tell Xactimate that the wall is a Containment Barrier.
You can also use the existing missing wall in the hall and into the Breakfast Nook and
any doors to create additional barriers.
If you need more barriers, add them all at once.
Once your Barriers are in place, you can move over to the XactScope tab.
The next step, is to add any objects that will be affected during the mitigation process,
such as lower kitchen cabinets…
And a sink…
As you place them, XactScope will start to add script cards and questions for the items
you are adding.
Almost any adjustment or change that needs to be made to selections added through XactScope
can be done on the Actions Tab.
With all the objects added, you can now add zones and affected areas.
Water Mitigation Zones allow you to tell Xactimate what Category and Class of water damage has
occurred and where.
For this example, it has been determined the water was category 2, gray water with a class
1 severity.
To create zones, select the Zone mode on the toolbar.
To add a zone, click the add icon, give it a name if needed, select the category and
class, and confirm your selections.
This first zone will be purple and selected rooms can be added to the zone.
The room color will now change to the selected zone.
More zones can be added as needed.
For this example, the water was primarily on the floor.
You can show affected floor areas 3 ways.
The entire room by using a double click, Click and drag to create a rectangle area,
Or Free form, to select a custom area.
Single click and then move the mouse to the next area and single click again.
After an affected area has been selected, the action questions change allowing you to
decide how damage for individual items will be handled.
You can also add affected areas to walls in 3D view.
And that’s how to get your Water Mitigation estimate started in XactScope.
Watch the Water Mitigation equipment and scripts using XactScope video to learn more about
XactScope.
You can also check out our training resources at xactware.com/training.
Fill out the survey below to let us know if there's anything you'd like to learn more
about.
And be sure to like this video and subscribe to our channel for more XpertTips each week.

metadata.shortDescription:
In today's video we look at 5 Xactimate hacks that will help you make more money and save time during the estimating process.

Xactimate is a robust tool but it can often times be overwhelming for a contractor when trying to write an water damage estimate.  We will explore some time saving techniques that allowed us to write a faster estimate that actually put more money in our pocket!


Want me to help you grow your restoration company?  


Go to www.WorkWithShane.com Fill out the form and let's get on a call!


HELP SPREAD THE WORD

If you are on facebook and are members of other restoration groups, please share this video so others can see it.


Restoration Rebels: https://www.facebook.com/groups/RestorationRebel

NORRP: https://www.facebook.com/groups/norrp

Truckmount Forums: https://www.facebook.com/groups/1375097549402700

--- Do you own a restoration company? ---

You NEED to see our legal document package.  You can see all the contracts and documents we use to run our restoration company here 
- www.RestorationContracts.com

Ever wonder if you are leaving money on the table when you are invoicing your jobs?  I bet you are!  Use our invoice checklist to make sure that you pick up every dollar that you deserve.  
- www.InvoiceChecklist.com

Have you joined our Facebook Group Restoration University?
Click the link to get access of our FREE TRAINING PROGRAM!
Join our Facebook Group: https://www.facebook.com/groups/restorationuniversity

If you aren't following me on Facebook yet, click this link to see new content:
Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/therestorationcontractor


Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/shaneodazier/

YouTube Video URL: https://youtu.be/xxY3mFNq9Gk

While this channel may earn minimal sums when the viewer uses the links, the viewer is in no way obligated to use these links. Thank you for your support!

"R&R Drywall" vs "Tear Out Wet Drywall and Bag for Disposal"
It seems like adjusters are using incorrect Xactimate line items most of the time, when estimating fire damage, water damage and even hurricane damage.

This is a sneak peak from the IES Certified Online Virtual Training Course. Keep grinding!

The full $200K startup budget and why only half of it needs to be cash
The exact equipment list to dry multiple houses at once.

Why a 2-person crew (crew chief + technician) can produce $1M/year
The "executive assistant as your clone" hire most owners skip
How to control your leads with one referral source before adding a second fishing hole. The truth about Xactimate, dry logs, TPAs, and who your customer really is.

metadata.title: The Water Damage Mitigation Process Step by Step by PuroClean
metadata.author: PuroClean of Central Southwest Houston
metadata.shortDescription: In this video, PuroClean of Central Southwest Houston walks you through the step-by-step process of water damage restoration — from emergency response and water removal to drying, sanitizing, and full repairs. See how our experts use advanced equipment and proven techniques to protect your property and bring it back to pre-loss condition.

segments.text: Hi, I'm Andrew Sanchez, production
manager of the mitigation department
here at Pure Oakland of Central
Southwest Houston. Water damage can come
from a number of sources, including
water heaters, burst supply lines, AC
condensation leaks, broken or leaking
pipes inside the walls, dishwasher,
washing machines, and even your sprinker
and irrigation system. Our number one
priority is response time. Once we
receive a job order from our
administration team, we have 4 hours to
arrive on site. By that time, I get the
work order. All the job information has
already been set up, and I dispatch one
of our train technicians right away. The
very first step is documentation. This
is critical for the insurance
compliance. We use our company phones to
capture photos and everything, moisture
readings, close-up of damage, damage
items, even 3D scans with Docky Sketch.
Every detail matter because it provides
proof to the insurance company.
Next, we identify the source of water
and trace the flow of water throughout
the property. Once we understand where
it's coming from and where it's
spreading, we determine the category of
the water damage. There are three main
categories. Category one, clean water
like a burst supply line.
Category two, water that started out
clean but has been sitting up to 48
hours like a washing machine overflow.
Category three, contaminated water such
as sewage and outside flood water.
Based on what we see during our
inspection, we create a preliminary
scope of work. Part of that involves
determining which materials are
salvageable and which materials are not.
For example, some flooring and cabinetry
may be saved, but others may need to be
removed.
We then contact the insurance carrier to
share our initial findings. If cabinetry
or flooring is required to be removed,
we will seek approval before performing
any demo.
Once approvals are in, we'll complete
the demo and begin the drying process by
setting specialized equipment like air
movers and dehumidifiers to restore the
property's environment safely.
Throughout the process, we document
everything to keep insurance carriers
informed and to protect the homeowner's
claim. Later, we'll use a program called
Exactate to build a detailed estimates,
but we'll cover that in a separate
video.
In short, our water mitigation process
is about fast response, thorough
documentation, and effective
restoration.
Whether the damage comes from a water
heater, an AC line, or a burst pipe, or
an appliance like a dishwasher, our team
is trained and ready to help.

metadata.title: IICRC S520 - Core Principle of Mould Remediation
metadata.author: Phill McGurk
metadata.shortDescription: The ANSI/IICRC S520 (2024) serves as a comprehensive procedural standard for the professional remediation of mold within indoor environments. It establishes a technical framework for restoring structures and contents to a normal fungal ecology, categorized as Condition 1, by emphasizing the physical removal of contamination rather than simply killing it with chemicals. The text outlines the critical roles of Indoor Environmental Professionals (IEPs) and remediators, detailing necessary engineering controls, such as containment and pressure differentials, to prevent the spread of spores. Beyond technical protocols, the document provides extensive guidance on risk management, specialized cleaning methodologies for various materials, and the administrative requirements for documentation and insurance. It ultimately advocates for a shift away from using the visible size of a mold colony to determine a response, focusing instead on scientific principles and standard of care to ensure occupant safety.

metadata.title: Mould Remediation Done Right: The Official IICRC S520 Homeowner Guide
metadata.author: Balanced Building Biology
metadata.shortDescription:
```
Is your home suffering from water damage or mould contamination? Before hiring a contractor or filing an insurance claim, you need to understand the official standard of care governing professional mould remediation [1-3]. 

In this comprehensive overview, we break down the AS-IICRC S520 (2024/2025) standard for professional mould remediation and the AS-IICRC S500 standard for water damage restoration [1, 2]. Learn why physical source removal is mandatory, why chemical sprays and fogging are not a primary solution, and how independent Building Biologists protect your rights and health [4-9].

---

⏱️ TIMESTAMPS / CHAPTERS
00:00 - Introduction: Why Proper Sequence Matters
01:15 - Water Damage vs. Mould: S500 (Drying) vs. S520 (Remediation) [1, 2]
02:40 - The Health Escalation Rule: When You Need an Independent IEP / Building Biologist [8-11]
04:10 - Phase 1: Emergency Source Control & Initial Assessment (24–48 Hours) [1, 12-14]
05:30 - Phase 2: Poly Containment & Maintaining -5 Pa Negative Air Pressure [15-20]
07:15 - Phase 3: Physical Removal & HEPA Decontamination (Why Bleach Fails) [4, 5, 21, 22]
08:50 - Phase 4: Psychrometric Structural Drying & Dehumidification [12, 23-26]
10:30 - Phase 5: Post-Remediation Evaluation (PRE) vs. Independent Clearance Verification (PRV) [27-31]
12:15 - Key Questions to Ask Your Remediator Before Signing

---

🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS & STANDARDS COVERED:
1. Physical Removal Over Sprays: Under S520 clause 2.1.1, physical source removal is the primary means of remediation [2, 5, 32]. Attempts to kill, fog, or encapsulate mould without physical removal constitute a formal deviation from the standard of care [4, 6, 7, 32, 33].
2. Containment & Engineering Controls: Contaminated materials must never be disturbed before establishing 6-mil fire-retardant poly containment, sealing HVAC grilles, and logging a minimum of -5 Pa (-0.02 in. w.c.) negative pressure with a manometer [15-20].
3. Health-Triggered Escalation: If occupants report health symptoms (e.g., asthma, allergies, or chronic fatigue), the project escalates to Recovery Level 2+, requiring an independent third-party Indoor Environmental Professional (IEP) or Building Biologist [8-11, 34, 35].
4. Verification Matters: Remediators perform an internal Post-Remediation Evaluation (PRE), but complex or health-related jobs require an independent Post-Remediation Verification (PRV) to confirm the return to Condition 1 (normal fungal ecology) [27-31].

---

📚 RESOURCES & DOCUMENTATION

• AS-IICRC S500: Standard for Professional Water Damage Restoration [1, 2]
```

metadata.shortDescription:
Learn more about the new edition of the best-selling ANSI/IICRC S500 Standard for Professional Water Damage Restoration.

Webinar hosted by: Brandon Burton, Larry Carlson, Darren Foote, Scott McFadzen, and Mili Washington.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

ABOUT THE IICRC

For five decades, the Institute of Inspection Cleaning and Restoration Certification (IICRC) has developed globally recognized Standards and Certifications for the Inspection, Cleaning, and Restoration Industries.
With industry-wide contributions and a commitment to quality, the IICRC offers 26 Certifications across divisions, three advanced Master Designations, and multiple pathways to build a career in-person and via live-stream.

For five decades, the Institute of Inspection Cleaning and Restoration Certification (IICRC) has developed globally recognized Standards and Certifications for the Inspection, Cleaning, and Restoration Industries.

metadata.title: Only Hire Certified Professionals! - (Water Restoration/IICRC s500 VS. Mold Remediation/IICRC s520)
metadata.author: Andrew Melrose
metadata.shortDescription:
IICRC S500 vs. IICRC S520 – What Homeowners MUST Know About Water Damage & Mold Remediation

If your home has suffered water damage or mold contamination, knowing the difference between (and importance of) the IICRC S500 Water Damage Restoration Standards and the IICRC S520 Mold Remediation Standards can save you thousands of dollars and protect your health.

🚨 NOT ALL CONTRACTORS FOLLOW THE RIGHT STANDARDS! 🚨
Some companies claim they can handle water damage cleanup or mold remediation, but if they’re not IICRC-certified and not following these strict industry standards, they could be doing more harm than good.

💡 Here’s What You’ll Learn in This Video:
✔️ The IICRC S500 – Water Damage Restoration: When, Why & How It’s Used
✔️ The IICRC S520 – Mold Remediation: Critical Differences from Water Damage Cleanup
✔️ Why These Standards Exist & How They Protect You, the Homeowner
✔️ How to Identify a Qualified Professional vs. a Contractor Cutting Corners
✔️ The Risks of Hiring an Unqualified Company (cross-contamination, health hazards, improper cleanup) 

⚠️ Water damage cleanup and mold remediation are NOT the same! Just because a company dries out your home after a flood does NOT mean they know how to properly remove mold and prevent further contamination.

🔑 KEY TAKEAWAY:
Always hire an IICRC-certified professional who follows the correct standard (S500 for water damage, S520 for mold remediation) to ensure your home is restored safely, effectively, and legally.

🔗 Resources & Ways to Work With Me:
📍 Website: www.melrosemoldsolutions.com
📍 Instagram: @melrosemoldsolutions
📍 1-on-1 Virtual Consulting: https://andrewmelrose.bloom.io/book
📍 Free Mold Safe Home Habits Guide: https://fierce-maker-7900.ck.page/freeguide
📍 Mold Removal Guide (Avoid Costly Mistakes!): https://fierce-maker-7900.ck.page/moldremoval

📢 Drop your questions in the comments below! Have you ever had an issue with an unqualified contractor? Let’s talk about it.

🔥 ...one more thing, it may not be best to always your insurance carriers "preferred vendor" ... see my other YouTube with Steve Gern about that as we expose the common tactics of the insurance companies and outline everything you need to know as a homeowner about navigating that process.

metadata.title: Inside the S520: The Standard That Changed Mold Remediation
metadata.author: ISSA Media
metadata.shortDescription:
Mold is no longer just a technical issue—it’s a public health, housing, and policy conversation. 

In this episode of Unscripted, an IICRC video production, leaders from the IICRC sit down to talk openly about mold, the evolution of the ANSI/IICRC S520 Standard for Professional Mold Remediation, and the organization’s role in training, certification, and advocacy.

The discussion traces the journey from early standards development to real-world adoption, including how IICRC guidance has informed conversations around military housing and mold-related legislation. 

The panel also explores what this growing visibility means for contractors, why training and documentation matter more than ever, and how standards help protect both occupants and professionals.

This episode offers a behind-the-scenes look at how industry leadership, education, and consensus-based standards work together to advance the mold remediation industry.

Learn more about the IICRC https://iicrc.org

#IICRC #Unscripted #MoldRemediation #S520 #Standards #Training #Certification #Advocacy #IndoorAirQuality #RestorationIndustry #EnvironmentalHealth #Leadership #MilitaryHousing

videos.full_text: When conversations around mold come up, they often focus on the problem. What went wrong? Who's at fault or that standards weren't followed? What we talk about less often is the long behindthe-scenes work required to raise the bar for an entire industry. That work doesn't happen overnight and it doesn't happen by accident. Today's conversation focuses on mold, not just as a technical issue, but as a leadership and advocacy story. >> [music] >> do this. I'm pleased to welcome three experts from the IICRC, Robbie Bradshaw, Holly Burns, and Mark Cornelius. Welcome everybody. It's great to have you on the program. >> Mark, >> we're going to start with you on our first question. Are you ready? >> I am Jeff. Thank you very much. if you could for people who may not know the history, how did the IICRC S520 come into existence and what problem was it originally designed to solve for the industry? >> Well, thank you Jeff. Um, obviously I'm Mark Cornelius. I've been in the cleaning and restoration industry now for right at 42 years. So, I've actually seen pretty much everything kind of come into play. Um, all the way from cleaning carpet to rebuilding buildings from the ground up. And I also have the honor and pleasure of uh serving on the board of directors with uh Dr. Harley Burns and um you know I've been on the board now for four years. So involved with quite a bit of stuff that's going on. So [clears throat] to your question about how the S520 was uh basically brought into being. Uh we have to first start with the S500 which was the uh standard that came out for the water damage restoration industry. But the S500 did not really address anything with mold. It it recognized and understood um that mold starts with water, but it really didn't have anything to do with real life uh world, you know, mold remediation challenges. The S520 um was developed primarily for mold remediation companies and the workers um along with you know experts and uh people like industrial hygienists and things and consultants but it was uh primarily developed for the contractor to be able to do the mold remediation side of it and Jeff you know mold's been a concern for hundreds of years if not thousands of years and it really started becoming prevalent in the United States around in the 1970s and 80s um when sick building syndrome first came out and then sick building syndrome kind of turned into you know basically toxic you know mold syndrome around the early 90s and then it kind of morphed into some of the other stuff where some of the early guidancees uh guidances dealt with situations involving like the health um care industry and u public health officials and stuff and I don't mean to use these words um in a uh in a bad way but there was a lot of hype there was a lot of heightened awareness there was sensationalism due to media there was some large you know litigation cases you know Aaron Brockovich Ed McMahon's dog um the Melinda Ballard uh situation and then the mold is gold and there you know mold's the next bestas and then every water job turned from a $2,000 job to a $40,000 job. And then there was the Cleveland, Ohio incident where there was about 37 babies, a cluster of babies that got sick. 12 of them died. The CDC came out. They made a bunch of comments and then in 2000, you know, they came back out and said that they actually didn't have a causal link to the deaths from it. So, there was a need for the restoration industry to have a standard. And um here's the thing. I don't know if you're aware of, Jeff, there's an actual King of the Hill episode that came out in 2003 dedicated to the mole remediation industry. >> I am not caught up on my King of the Hill episodes, so I need to do that. Mark, obviously, >> season 8, episode 6. >> Okay, I'll write that down. There we go. Thank you, Mark. A great introduction and comment there. Um, Holly, let's go to you from the work you do. Kind of the same question. Anything to add there about the history and how maybe you use the S520 as well. >> So, uh, thank you for having me here. I am very honored to be here with some with these astounding people, but um, my name is Dr. Holly Burns. I al also am a board on the board of directors and I've been in restoration uh for nearly 20 years doing restoration and managing a restoration company and then owning my own indoor air company. So, uh right now we do assessments and I also train for the AMRT, WRT, ASD and now the HST courses. The S520 was born out of necessity uh because before it existed, mold remediation was largely inconsistent. Methods varied widely and documentation was uneven. So there was very little alignment between what the contractors did and what building science supported. So from an assessment standpoint, this really or that at that particular time really created a risk. And so the S520 was developed and established as a science-based consensus standard that defined what's reasonable and appropriate remediation and actually what does that look like grounded in exposure control management and occupant safety. So at the end of the day what are we really looking at? We're looking at the health of the occupants and the structural stability of that property, which I believe is the most important asset many people have is their home and then more importantly their health. >> And Robbie, uh, I don't think you're a mold assessor or inspector or worker. Introduce yourself and tell us what you think about this as well and the S520, what that means to you and the work you do. >> So, thanks Jeff for having me again. My name is Robbie Branch. I'm the uh director of government relations for the IICRC. Um and uh one of the I think the important aspect of the S520 from my standpoint um is I think every legislator that I have ever talked to has received at least one call from a constituent complaining about mold in some capacity. And almost every single time they have no idea how to address it. They don't know what to say back to the constituent. They believe that the industry is regulated even though it's not. They you know so they don't they never know and so I I tell them is you know there are certifications there is a standard of care for the industry and um it's you it's extremely helpful because once they hear that there's a standard of care for the industry that's when they their eyes open they're like okay so there is an answer to my constituents question now how do we address that and we go from there. Thank you, Robbie. Back to you, Mark, on this next question. Uh, we know that standards don't write themselves. We also know they change over time. Let's let's talk about that. What have you seen with the S520? How it's changed or evolved? And what does that look like when things change like the science, that technology, maybe the work done to remove mold? Well, Jeeoff, that's uh that's a million-dollar question there because um every time the standard gets revised and there's a new opinion about um a change in science or risk factors, um I've not met a single person yet who serves on a standards consensus body that's not passionate about something. And even though we do our best to make sure that we're bringing um um actual um citable outside sources to it, um there's a lot of opinion that gets introduced um into it as well. So it it takes a lot of time to um get to the bottom of it and it can be heated. it can be contentious and um that just goes to show that all of the sides are trying to bring um what's best for the industry, not just it being one-sided. So there it can take time. You know, the original S520 took uh almost three years, a little over three years for 14 uh volunteers to bring the first edition out. But interestingly, it can take even longer sometimes like the um the last version of the S540, the trauma standard took uh two plus years just to revise the original standard because there are a lot of times some changes and maybe new OSHA regulations or health and safety concerns um or a new technology and just because there's a new chemical out on the market sometimes, you know, magic potions, doesn't mean that it's suitable um for the industry. So, it it's a it's quite a um labor of love to determine if it is going to actually be applicable um to what we're doing because we're trying to leave the customer in a in a safe and healthy environment. >> Holly, anything to add to what Mark just said there? >> So, I think one of the most important things to understand is that the S520 is a living standard. So as remediators and assessors, we see firsthand how building materials, moisture dynamics, and occupant vulnerability change over time. And so the ICRC updates the S520 through a structured consensus process like Mark was talking about that includes researchers, clinicians, remediators, and risk professionals. So when new when new science emerges whether it's about aerosolization immuno compromised individuals and occupants equipment or containment effectiveness it's evaluated it's debated like Mark was talking about with the 14 people um that had a hand in it and integrated thoughtfully and not reactively. >> Let's stick with you on this question then we'll go to Mark and then my next question after that is all about the legal stuff. So Robbie, we'll tee you up there. But Holly, thinking about IICC training, which you and Mark both do, but thinking about that, how does it translate what's written in the S520 into practical, defensible decisions contractors can make in the field and rely on in the field? >> And Jeff, really, this is where training is critical because the IICRC, the S520, isn't just a checklist. It's a decision making framework standard. And so in training like Mark does uh we both do, we teach professionals how to interpret conditions, assess the risk and justify their approach. And I always say justify justify every decision you make based on the principles rather than any shortcuts. From an assessor's or a remediator standpoint, this is actually huge. Because as you mentioned, Jeff, the defensibility that comes from being able to explain why a method was selected and not just that it was done. >> Mark, I know you're chomping at the bit to get into that. What would you say? >> Uh, thank you, Jeff. And and I, you know, Dr. Burns really said quite a good amount of information there. And, you know, as she stated, I I teach a lot of AMRT courses. I actually have six different subject matters that I deliver for IICC. Um, and you know, WRT is one of them. But IC approved instructors that deliver IC approved courses are supposed to bring the principles set forth in the standards to real world practice. Um, this is also based off of the instructor's experience in the field. Um, so if you've got an instructor who's got a lot of, like Holly said, 20 years experience in it, it's it it's not that hard to bring it forward into it. But the the courses are developed through what's called a CPD, the certification program description. That's based off of what the standard brings forward. Um, plus additional stuff that that instructor brings into it from their personal experience. So the contractor should also understand that when doing mold remediation though the S500 is also still applicable uh because the only reason you have water I mean mold is because you have water. So, one of the biggest misconceptions in my opinion, I'll try to wrap this up really quick, is um maybe it's just a pick on words, but a lot of restoers use the standard to defend their actions when in my opinion, I use the standard to judge my decisions prior to doing the job. And then therefore, if they're sound to the standard, then I don't have to defend anything. So the training basically is based off of the understanding of that standard. >> Robbie, this one's for you. We know that mold has increasingly become a public health and housing issue, uh not just a restoration issue, but talk about this. When did the IICRC begin to recognize that its standards and expertise could play a bigger role beyond the job site and in your world, especially in policy and legislative conversations? Um, so I mean I was hired on in 2021 with the idea that we were going to build up the IIC advocacy department that we were going to create it. Um, but I think IC standards, especially the S520, found its way into legislation, you know, back in 2007 in Kentucky. Um, and that was without any sort of, from my understanding, any sort of, you know, push from the ICRC. Um so I think that that the leadership at the time had realized that okay we you know this is something that we need to do. Um our standards need to be recognized our certifications need to be recognized. Um and obviously like you said mold is one of the larger policy issues that we are seeing. And so that is probably I would say 75% of my conversations with policy makers is about mold and mold remediation. And so the S520 and the AMRT and the MRS get brought up a lot in conversation. Um and again the the policy makers are excited that there is something out there that they don't have to reinvent the wheel. Um and uh and we've been successful. >> Can you talk a little bit about how you introduce those thoughts to these policy makers? Like what do those conversations sound like? Do you meet them in the hallway in Washington? Are you sending off some some emails? What does that look like? Uh it's a mixture. Um you know we attend conferences where state legislators are at. Um and we have a lot of conversations there. Um we have conversations in DC uh on Capitol Hill. Um and then sometimes it's just like this very just Zoom calls. Um and uh a lot of the times there will be consumers that have had bad experiences with non-certified mold remediators who weren't following the standard. And you know, they were like, "It's a long shot, but we keep hearing about it." metadata.title: Texas Mold Remediation:  IICRC S520/R520, IICRC S500 and the TMARR
metadata.author: Time's Dark Captains
metadata.shortDescription:
After the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation (TDLR) took over the Texas Mold Program, changes were made to the program and to the state licensing tests for mold to de-emphasize the EPA Mold in Commercial Buildings and Schools guidance and emphasize the IICRC mold remediation and water response standards.  This resulted in mold training providers having an increased focus on the IICRC standards within in training classes.  The TDLR misrepresented to the Texas Senate and House that the IICRC standards were "certifications" and constituted "training" as well.  The IICRC S520 dispels that in the foreword of the book.

These actions has now made the IICRC the emerging "state standard" by default, and many remediators are quoting or stating outright that they are "following the IICRC S520" when in fact many have not read it or follow the contents.  In this video I will address the unique paring of the elements of  TMARR and the IICRC Standards which actually results in a "suprecharged upgrade" for the Texas Mold Remediation and Assessment industry.  For those outside of Texas, this video addresses the basic requirements of the standard.  All the information is read directly from the IICRC documents and page numbers are referred to.

No more calling it a "water event" only, without addressing the mold and other environmental or hazard issues.  This video has a companion video that addresses the asbestos and lead paint issues as well.

metadata.title: POV: Applied Structural Drying with RTI | IICRC ASD Course with Destry Ransdell
metadata.author: Restoration Technical Institute
metadata.shortDescription:
Take a POV trip into Restoration Technical Institute's very own "Flood House" Located in Reading Pennsylvania, where we show our students *firsthand* what it's like to dry an actual structure on the job. Our experienced instructor, Destry Ransdell, as well as our very own John Perella take you through the flood house while instructing ambitious, determined students on how to properly dry a structure after a flood/extensive water damage has taken place. This course is an IICRC certified class.

Restoration Technical Institute is dedicated to teaching the future leaders of the restoration and construction industries; hosting live classes with vetted instructors, online classes for those who wish to learn from the comfort of their own homes, and supplies a revolutionary Digital Training Solution that gives any restoration company the ability to train their employees, and expand capabilities as a company. Visit us at www.RTILearning.com

Follow our other social medias!
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/rtilearning/
Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/RestorationTechnicalInstitute
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/restoration-technical-institute/
Our Tiktok: https://www.tiktok.com/@rtilearning1145?is_from_webapp=1&sender_device=pc

The best Xactimate training for all users is HERE:    https://www.estimatetv.com 

Get the Level 1 Practice Exam HERE:  https://drive.google.com/file/d/1R-oKs7JYWTy-i5u6S5YzpXCXcsMmYw8l/view?usp=sharing

Ready to take it to the next level?  Get complete Level 1 Xactimate User Certification prep training HERE:  https://www.adjustertv.com/en/xactimate-certification

🔍 Xactimate Line Items: The Essential Guide to Finding Materials & Repairs (Search Tutorial)

Have you ever struggled to find the right materials or repairs (known as line items) in Xactimate? This video is your complete guide to quickly and accurately locating everything you need—from paint to insulation—to build your estimate.

📝 Setting Up the Estimate

We begin by demonstrating a crucial step: setting up a room with dimensions in your estimate (e.g., a 12' x 10' "Bedroom"). This ensures that when you add a line item, Xactimate automatically calculates the exact quantity needed, saving you time and preventing errors.

🔑 Two Ways to Find Line Items

We walk you through the two most efficient ways to search:

Using the Search Pane: Learn how to find the dedicated Search tab, enter descriptive words like "paint," and navigate the Item Search Results to select the specific line item you need (e.g., "Paint, 1 Coat [V]").

Pro Tip: Master Category Codes: This is the fastest way to work in Xactimate! We teach you the fundamental Category Codes (like PNT for Paint, INS for Insulation, DRY for Drywall, and RFG for Roofing). By typing these codes directly into the selector box, you can instantly filter the entire database and refine your search using keywords (like "bat" or "foil") to find the precise item you need. 


https://www.adjustertv.com/en/xactimate-certification

metadata.shortDescription:
Join Whatley and Fletcher as they dive into the newest additions and modifications in the May 2026 Xactimate Price List update. There are some BIG changes this month you won’t want to miss! Xactware updates regional price lists every month; we provide the context and perspective you need to understand why these items were added and, more importantly, how to use them.

ADVANCE THE CAUSE: Is there a line item that doesn’t exist yet but should? We advocate for the adoption of line items that help contractors and adjusters settle claims quickly and fairly. If you’re performing an activity in the field that lacks a dedicated line item, let us know here:  https://getinsights.org/advance-the-cause/line-item-request

OPTIMIZE YOUR ESTIMATES We believe that identifying the line items that most accurately represent cost and scope is the key to generating estimates that get approved without hesitation.

View Past Summaries: See all previous price list updates here: https://getinsights.org/resources/price-list-update-summary

💬 JOIN THE CONVERSATION Do you have questions, tips, or ideas about Xactimate price lists? What is the most frustrating "missing" line item in your current workflow? Let us know in the comments below!

ABOUT ACTIONABLE INSIGHTS Actionable Insights is a foundation dedicated to preserving the health of the property insurance ecosystem by advancing education and clarifying globally recognized billing standards.

metadata.title: How to Prove an Insurance Estimate Wrong — Line by Line in Xactimate
metadata.author: American Roof Supplements
metadata.shortDescription:
👉 Your first Xactimate estimate or supplement is FREE. Book a 10-minute setup call with Joe: https://bit.ly/ARS-FreeSupplement
No monthly fees, no minimums. Pay per job: $50 per estimate, $150 per supplement.

As a roofing contractor, how do you show where an insurance estimate differs from the construction scope your roof project requires? In this video, we walk through a residential roof estimate line by line in Xactimate, focusing on documentation rather than arguments over the final dollar amount.

We use a composite, illustrative roof file—not a documented claim against a specific carrier. The example amounts and conditions are illustrative, and no actual claim approval or payment outcome is being presented.

You will see how an estimate can look complete while still requiring closer review of materials, quantities, and construction operations:

• Shingle type and roofing materials
• Tear-off layers and how the selected removal item accounts for them
• Starter shingles and supporting product requirements
• Hip and ridge measurements
• Drip edge and applicable, supported code requirements
• Underlayment materials, quantities, and installation scope
• Step flashing, roof-to-wall flashing, and roof penetrations
• Roof ventilation components and quantities
• Decking conditions documented after tear-off
• Measurements, photos, product information, and relevant supporting documents
• Carrier estimate vs. contractor-supported construction scope
• Item inclusions and overlapping charges to check before adding scope

The goal is not to assume the adjuster is wrong. It is to identify legitimate differences and make each requested correction easy to review. Check what is already included before adding a separate charge, and connect each proposed change to clear evidence.

When your homeowner asks why your estimate differs from the carrier's, explain the documented construction requirements without promising a larger payment. Necessary construction work—including decking replacement—does not automatically establish insurance coverage.

American Roof Supplements prepares residential Xactimate estimates, supplements, and supporting documentation. We document legitimate construction scope with measurements, photos, product information, notes, and supported construction or code-related operations.

American Roof Supplements is not a public-adjusting company or law firm. Supplements do not create coverage, change the deductible, turn actual-cash-value coverage into replacement-cost coverage, make nonrecoverable depreciation recoverable, or guarantee approval. The carrier determines coverage; policy interpretation, claim negotiation, public adjusting, and legal representation stay with the appropriate licensed professional.

Your first estimate or supplement is free. After that, a residential Xactimate estimate is $50, and a standalone supplement is $150. If ARS prepared the estimate for that same job, the follow-up supplement is $100.

There is no monthly fee, no minimum number of jobs, and reasonable revisions are included. Newer roofing contractors receive extra guidance through their first five claims, with ongoing support afterward.

Use the link at the top of the description to book your 10-minute setup call with Joe.

Share this with your roofing team or roofing WhatsApp or Facebook group, and subscribe for more practical roofing, Xactimate, supplement, and claim-documentation content.

Contractors: if you don't know how much insurance companies pay for property repairs, you aren't generating the correct amount of income.
Over 80% of insurance companies - including State Farm, Farmers, Allstate, USAA, Nationwide, MetLife, Liberty Mutual, Safeco, The Hartford, American Family, ASI, American Modern, QBE and many more - use the industry standard pricing software called Xactimate.

Q) What is Xactimate?

A) Xactimate is a third-party software made by Xactware, owned by Verisk. Xactware conducts extensive market research and comes up with a price for almost every conceivable item in construction. This includes variables for labor, material, equipment, general site conditions and general contractor's overhead and profit.

Xactimate has a separate pricelist for different markets. San Diego has a different pricelist than Los Angeles; Miami has a different pricelist than Orlando, and so on.
Even more significant, Xactimate changes all pricelists once per month. Every month, the price to remove and replace one linear foot of fascia changes, for example.

Sometimes it changes a little and sometimes it changes a LOT.

This isn't always a great thing for contractors as sometimes it goes down. However, after a hail storm, hurricane, large flood or other natural disaster which affects an entire market, usually -generally speaking- the pricelist for that market will go up in the next monthly pricelist update. It could even take two months or longer for the software to reflect the true market data.

For example, look no further than the recent April 2016 massive hails storms in North Texas, which affected the Dallas Fort Worth market.

Most professionals in the industry were fairly confident that the May 2016 pricelist would show an increase because of the direct market impact. It was afterall a multi-billion dollar event. Contractors were reporting that their material suppliers and subcontractors were sending out letters notifying their customers of price increases across the board. Reports were coming in of the unavailability of roofers and gutter installers.

However, in the May pricelist... nothing.

Sure,  it went up by a couple of dollars here and there but not enough to really impact most estimates as a whole.

Some were rather disappointed but it seems they weren't alone.

Later in May, the North Texas Roofing Contractors Association (NTRCA) sent out an email to its members alerting them to this issue, along with a proposed solution to attempt to resolve it. The NTRCA members were encouraged to send an email to Xactware to voice their displeasure, and to share any info (from suppliers, subcontractors, etc) with Xactware that could possibly contribute to a resolution.

In June: major difference! Most estimates in this market went up significantly. And the July and August updates also saw slight increases. Great job NTRCA and its members for following through!

See the above video to see a specific example of a real claim in live action.

We had written an Xactimate estimate for our contractor client for a hail damage claim in the DFW market. Our estimate was already completed and we simply updated it from the May 2016 pricelist to the August 2016 pricelist.

It resulted in over a $2,600.00 increase! What can your company do with an extra $2,600?

The above described issue highlights the fact that it's imperative to have experts on your side to help you navigate the complex waters of insurance repair estimating.

If you don't present your estimates in Xactimate, you're losing.

If you don't have Xactimate experts creating your Xactimate estimates, you're failing.

The obvious solution is definitely to turn to the leader in Xactimate estimate writing & invoicing service in the United States and Canada:

https://www.OverheadAndProfit.com

Visit us today to see what we can do for your business!

metadata.title: Roofer Explains Roofing Terms: 12 Roof Components That Matter in Xactimate
metadata.author: American Roof Supplements
metadata.shortDescription:
👉 Your first Xactimate estimate or supplement is FREE. Book a 10-minute setup call with Joe: https://bit.ly/ARS-FreeSupplement
No monthly fees, no minimums. Pay per job: $50 per estimate, $150 per supplement.

Do you know all the roof components that should be documented in an Xactimate roof estimate? From roof pitch and drip edge to ridge caps, flashing, and pipe boots, understanding roofing terms is essential for contractors preparing accurate roof estimates and supplements.

In this video, we explain 12 important roof component checkpoints, what each one does, where to find it, and how roofing contractors can measure and document it for an accurate scope of work.

You'll learn about roof slope and pitch, eaves and rakes, drip edge, starter strips, roof underlayment, ice and water barrier, valleys, hips and ridges, roof decking, pipe boots, roof ventilation, and flashing.

We also explain how measurements, inspection photos, roof diagrams, and installation requirements help support legitimate roofing operations in Xactimate.

Whether you're an experienced roofer, a roofing sales representative, or a contractor new to insurance restoration, this guide will help you better understand roof anatomy and organize your documentation.

Not every component is required in every repair. Actual construction conditions, manufacturer specifications, applicable building codes, and the scope of damage must be considered.

**ABOUT AMERICAN ROOF SUPPLEMENTS**

American Roof Supplements prepares residential Xactimate estimates, supplements, and supporting documentation. We document legitimate construction scope with measurements, photos, product information, notes, and supported construction or code-related operations.

American Roof Supplements is not a public-adjusting company or law firm. Supplements do not create coverage, change the deductible, turn actual-cash-value coverage into replacement-cost coverage, make nonrecoverable depreciation recoverable, or guarantee approval. The carrier determines coverage; policy interpretation, claim negotiation, public adjusting, and legal representation stay with the appropriate licensed professional.

#RoofingTerms #RoofComponents #Xactimate

segments.text: Picture this. You finish inspecting a
storm damaged roof, send over your
measurements and open the estimate. The
shingles are there, but something feels
wrong. There is no starter strip. The
ridge vent is missing. Nobody accounted
for the flashing where the roof meets
the wall.
Three small details and suddenly the
estimate no longer describes the roof
you actually inspected. Here is the
dangerous part. If you cannot name a
component, measure it, and explain why
it belongs in the scope, you might never
notice it is absent. Today we walk from
edge to peak through 12 component
checkpoints that matter in Exactimate.
First, understand the roof itself. A
roof is not just one flat rectangle
covered in shingles. It is a collection
of planes, edges, intersections, and
penetrations. Those shapes control how
materials are installed, how water
travels, and how quantities are
calculated. Even accurate shingle area
cannot describe everything around it. So
as we go, remember four questions for
every component. What is it? Where is
it? How do you measure it? And what
documentation supports including it in
this particular job?
Checkpoint one. Roof slope and pitch.
Point to a single flat section of roof
that is a roof plane, sometimes called a
facet. Pitch describes how steep it is,
usually as inches of rise for every 12
inches of horizontal run. A 6 12 roof
rises 6 inches for every 12 inches
across. Pitch affects the true surface
area and steeper roofs may require
different labor considerations. Do not
eyeball it from the driveway. Use
reliable measurements, confirm varying
slopes, and record them clearly.
Measurement reports must match the
building. Aerial measurements can help,
but field conditions still control. Pay
attention to additions, dormers, and
different pitches on the same house.
Checkpoint two. The eaves and rakes.
These are not interchangeable. The eave
is the lower, generally horizontal edge
where water runs off the roof. The is
the sloped edge along a gable end. Trace
both in different colors on screen. Why
separate them?
Because materials at the eave and rake
can have different installation
requirements, and each edge has its own
linear footage.
Photograph the perimeter and keep the
measurements separate. Rake footage is
not single square footage. Checkpoint
three, drip edge. This is the metal
edging that helps direct water away from
the roof deck and fascia at exposed roof
edges. On a finished roof, it can be
easy to overlook from an aerial image.
Get an edge close-up. Identify the metal
profile, note where it is installed, and
measure the applicable eave and rake
lengths. Verify that roofs required
assembly. A drip edge is a real
component, but its presence alone does
not mean every claim automatically pays
for replacing it. Checkpoint four,
starter strip. Before the main field
shingles go down, a starter course is
installed at the edges as part of the
roofing system.
Its placement and sealant help protect
vulnerable shingle edges against wind
uplift. It differs from field shingles.
Look at the manufacturer's installation
instructions.
Document which edges need starter,
measure the appropriate linear footage,
and make sure your estimate reflects the
actual product and installation method.

metadata.title: Commercial Roof Coating | Hail Damage
metadata.author: Chad Michael - The Practitioner
metadata.shortDescription:
More content from yesterday in El Paso, TX. What to do when you find damage to the COATING, and the insurance company doesn't want to pay for the layers beneath... more building code info... dealing with "water-soaked underlayment and roof coverings"... how to include multiple roofing layers in the Xactimate estimate... how to include the agent in the process... how to avoid discussing policy and/or coverage... using drones for hail damage inspections. 👊😎

#ThePractitioner #InTheTrenches #ElPracticante

Strategy. Consistency. Diligence. Dedication. And most importantly of all, putting in the HARD WORK... that's REQUIRED... to WIN IN THIS GAME!

Inside a consulting meeting with my client, a contractor in the roofing business. Most roofing contractors don't send their Xactimate roof estimates to the correct place! This goes beyond roofing sales and will help to set you apart from the average insurance restoration contractor or roofing contractor.

We also cover an in-depth look at roof supplementing -from start to finish- including integrating building codes into your Xactimate estimate, the structure of the Xactimate estimate and talking with insurance adjusters during the insurance restoration supplementing process.

metadata.shortDescription:
Running a restoration company isn’t easy. From losing key partnerships to rebuilding your lead pipeline, every restorer eventually faces moments that test both their business and their values.

In this episode of the After Hours Podcast, we sit down with Rowdy Legg of Homeway Construction & Restoration to talk about how he rebuilt his company and scaled from $0 to $11M in just three years. We break down real strategies restorers are using today — from plumber referral networks and neighborhood marketing to the hard lessons of scaling fast.

If you're a restoration contractor looking to grow your water mitigation business, generate more leads, and avoid costly mistakes, this conversation is packed with insights you can apply immediately.

In this episode we cover:
-How plumber relationships generate consistent water damage jobs
-What it really takes to scale a restoration company to $10M+
-The biggest mistakes restorers make when growing too fast
-Why knowing your numbers can make or break your business
-Hard leadership decisions that come with scaling a company

Whether you're starting a water damage restoration company or trying to scale your mitigation business, this episode delivers real lessons from someone who’s been through it.

Book a demo of Albi — the restoration software built by restorers:
https://bit.ly/3T6x0Yo

Albi helps restoration companies streamline operations, document jobs faster, and get paid sooner so you can focus on growing your business.

metadata.shortDescription:
You Play to Win the (TPA) Game
The DYOJO Podcast LIVE, Episode 58
aka Pro vs. Joe 012
Recorded LIVE - Saturday, April 17, 2021 - 8pm PST

SPONSOR
The DYOJO Podcast is sponsored by Enlightened Restoration Solutions (ERS). Ben Justesen and his team have put together a dynamic live class which reviews real world estimates and elevates your ability to master the methodology of Xactware. Including how to determine your own labor rates, create your own price list, and navigate pricing feedback. -www.enlightenedrestorationsoluitons.com 

CO-HOST
Bryan Close
All American Restoration Services (Tacoma, WA) 

GUEST 1 
Tye Panzone (Bonney Lake, WA) 
TPA Repairs
* Taking a "no name" local contractor from the "back woods" of the PNW to a perennial Contractor Connection Top Contender 
* Can you make money doing program work? 
* Leveraging your TPA connections to build your book of business 
* Attracting a national brand to help repeat "success"

GUEST 2 
David Smith (Eugene, OR) 
TPA Mitigation
* Currently recovering from TPA work
* The best compliance person I have ever worked with  

Join us live - youtube.com/thedyojo

metadata.title: Running a TPA (Third Party Administrator) RFP Process That Is Less of a Wild West Fiduciary Shootout
metadata.author: Relentless Health Value
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode, host Stacey Richter delves into the complexities of the Third Party Administrator (TPA) Request for Proposal (RFP) process with guest Claire Brockbank from 32BJUnion. Episode 453.

The discussion highlights the critical role of contracts in managing health plans effectively and the potential pitfalls of accepting contracts crafted by TPAs without thorough review. Drawing from Claire's experience, they explore tactics like starting with your own contract paper in RFP processes to gain negotiation leverage, and the benefits of employer coalitions in navigating health care complexities. 

Real-world examples underscore the financial impacts of poorly negotiated contracts and highlight successful strategies for health plan sponsors to optimize costs and services. The episode aims to empower employers with tools and insights to negotiate effectively and ensure their health plan contracts align with their strategic goals, ultimately paving the way for better population health management and cost-effective care delivery.

Really probe on who they are accountable to and or beholden to. Make sure you ask those questions and hopefully loyalty to your broker consultant proves to be well founded, but you might be surprised how often there are conflicts and you again know those conflicts so that you can manage them as a savvy buyer. This is a whole can of worms and topic unto itself. There's a lot going on. Be really aware of it. That is just a magic word for anyone in the industry to say to put a halt on change. There's some quote, I'm going to butcher it. It's something like, listen to what they're telling you. They are telling you what's going on. Listen. There's just like a lot of factors here. That I think that the self-insured employers who are really knowledgeable about what's going on are fully aware of and certainly the benefit consultants, et cetera, who are listening to the show are even more aware of. I think what you're trying to do, this is true of any change in healthcare, you're trying to stack the deck in your favor. And that's the best you can do. The whole idea being, get the right people with the right expertise who know a lot about this and maybe you can pull from the coalitions for sure. Listen to the show there. I totally agree with you. There's a lot of very smart people who could add a lot of value into a formal or informal kind of board of advisors, if you will, you know, or RFP board of advisors that can work together, so the two things can happen. You sort of need your own people who are patting you on the shoulder and, and keeping your confidence and your inspiration up to move forward. I think there's one other thing too, Stacey, and that's that right now, I wish this weren't true, but this is still unusual. There's a cadre of people there, you know, they're your people who are listening to your podcast and most of us have a sort of evangelical zeal about this. So this is the time to ask for help. I reach out to people that I hear on your podcast or on Dave Chase's material, wherever. And because there's still a relatively small cadre, nobody will not offer to help. So take advantage of that. But the silver lining part of that is there are fellow travelers out there who would like to see the crowd get bigger. I love how you put that. That is so inspirational and it is a large reason why I started talking about the Relentless Health Value tribe because this is a community of very dedicated, driven individuals who are trying to do the right thing. And I think sometimes we, I'm so glad that you brought that up, Claire, because I think sometimes that is forgotten. Something that you had said earlier, I also just want to highlight here, especially relative to the attorneys. that someone may be using. And so if you stop and say, we're doing something different and this is why. It's really, really important because you will then get a read on your attorney earlier in the process. And, and then again, you have to decide at least knowing the biases are really important and or deciding that the biases are too great and you need somebody different. So if we're kind of recapping where we are in this conversation, the stepwise approach here is as you enter the RFP season, if you will, try to start with your own paper. Because if you write your own contract and then get respondents to edit what you have, then you have all of the advantages that we talked about earlier. You can get an example contract from the 32BJ website as at least a starting point and again, we will link to that in the show notes. It could be some variation of the fiduciary committee or some kind of board of advisors that you have assembled to help you through this process. It also should probably include an attorney and probably some other job descriptions and you're going to rely on them for IQ, but then also for inspiration and emotional support. In addition, you may be able to get help from coalitions and others what does good look like, right? Like, so say I am large or small and I actually go down this route, what do I consider especially first time out? What is success? How does it appear? That is a great question. And my team always laughs at me because I'm always telling them, don't let perfect be the enemy of good. You won't get all of what you ask for. You may get a third of what you ask for, but I think some of your speakers have talked about each concession that is made to you as a purchaser is a step down the path. So be happy with a third of it if you want. You've sent the message to the vendor community that you are paying attention. This is an incremental process. You know, you are trying to change the dynamics of what, 20 percent of our economy, but what I would also really stress, it would be good for you to do because it'll help you measure your progress. We have maybe a dozen bullet points of things that we weren't getting, that our contract limited us to, and we sort of tracked what we ended up with. We did focus on what we didn't get, but we said, wow. We have full data ownership now. We have this, we have that. So celebrate your victories, but also know you just are only going to get a portion of them. But next time around, you'll get more. And because you got a portion of them, the next employer will get that one easily, more easily, and they may get a new one. So just think of it as very, very incremental. I love how you, you said that this is not going to be like, we're going to take the mountain in the next five days. This is more of a, it's a little bit of a slog. It's incremental. And it also is one of those tipping point kinds of things where if people around you, if other employers or if everyone starts to ask for the same things, then it becomes easier for everybody. So what it also enables you to do is really have a clear eyed vision at the really important things that you want to focus on and pay attention there. So you may not get everything, but as long as you get some portion of your really important things, it actually could have an outsized impact on what you're trying to do with your plan. Claire Brockbank, is there anything I neglected to ask you that you think is important to add here? I think there's one other thing, and that's that as a strategy person and as the person who likes to commit to change, you get to that contract and you think, all right, what do we do next? But you can't stop there. So it's really important. You've gotten this change, right, in your purchasing relationship with your ASO, and you are going to have to keep holding their feet to the fire. You're going to have to keep setting in place the milestones where you're going to double check that in the contract you said you would do this. Are you doing it? Especially the things that maybe you had to dicker over, right? You have to police this. They are not going to because they're not vested. Many of these things they don't particularly want to do. So it's really important to not stop just before the finish line, if you will. And I definitely hear you, you know, because additionally, this might be something that that carrier ASO doesn't typically commit to. So trying to rely on their internal processes to make sure that your contract is adequately adjudicated as per the terms of the contract, you can see how that might be an issue. Even with the best of intention. So they're committed to it, but you're right. It's that these are not typical processes. It gets turned over to the ops team. They didn't understand what was going on. So you have to, A, you have to engage in a partnership. You've picked a partner. It shouldn't be an adversarial relationship, but you've picked a partner and you've asked them to do something different. So keep them honest. And this is just part of purchasing discipline. Do you know what I'm saying? So like, I guess it's how I in a way would sum up the last point that you're making, which is a really good one, is that, you know, the customer has to, is part of ensuring that the agreed upon contract is fully delivered upon. Exactly. Claire Brockbank, where would you direct people to go for more information? And one of those links is going to be to the sample contract, but is there anywhere else that you would direct people? I would direct them to our 32BJ Health Insights website where we have a number of tools for employers. Thank you, Stacey. This was so exciting. I'm such a fan. This is Shawn Grimminger, President and CEO of the National Alliance of Healthcare Purchaser Coalitions. If you like this podcast, I strongly recommend subscribing and leaving a review.

metadata.title: Understanding Third-Party Administrators (TPAs) in Healthcare Insurance
metadata.author: Navigating the Business of Medicine
metadata.shortDescription:
In today's video, we dive into the world of Third-Party Administrators, commonly known as TPAs, in healthcare insurance. If you've ever been puzzled by your insurance card saying one thing but having to deal with another company for claims and administrative matters, you're not alone. TPAs play a significant role in managing insurance plans for big employers and self-insured companies. 

Join us as we unravel the complexities, discuss their benefits, and provide insights into navigating this aspect of the healthcare industry. 

If you have questions or experiences with TPAs, please share them in the comments, and don't forget to like, subscribe, and share this video with your fellow healthcare professionals. Healthcare can be challenging, but we can make it a bit clearer together. Stay informed and take care!

Hi there! My name is Jennifer. Over the last 15 years, I've gained much experience working in the medical field in various roles. Through my experience, I've seen many medical practice owners make mistakes in running their businesses. That's why I created this channel - to help medical practice owners avoid these common pitfalls. I aim to promote growth and success within the private practice world of medicine. I believe healthcare has become too institutionalized, creating many unnecessary challenges and demands.

New to claims adjusting? Wondering whether to work for State Farm or Sedgwick? In this video, we break down the key differences between working for a carrier vs. a TPA — including training, claims types, flexibility, and career growth.

metadata.title: What All Roofing Contractors Need to Know About Adjusters
metadata.author: Chris Zimmerman
metadata.shortDescription:
Public adjuster vs. insurance adjuster: what's the difference, and when should you hire a public adjuster for an insurance claim?

In this video, I break down the different types of insurance adjusters roofing contractors work with, including staff adjusters, independent adjusters, CAT adjusters, and third-party ladder assist companies.

I'll explain who hires each adjuster, what authority they have during a roof insurance claim, and why understanding their role matters when working with homeowners and insurance companies.

We'll also cover public adjuster fees, letters of representation, and the potential risks of bringing in a public adjuster too early. Sometimes hiring one makes sense. Other times, you may be better off helping the homeowner work through the claim before taking that step.

The goal is to understand your options, stick to the facts, and help homeowners make informed decisions about their insurance claims.

VIDEO CHAPTERS

00:00 Introduction: Types of Adjusters
00:13 Public vs. Insurance Adjusters: Who They Represent
00:30 Insurance Adjusters: Roles and Responsibilities
01:01 Staff Adjusters
01:16 Independent Adjusters
01:52 CAT Adjusters: Responding to Major Storms
02:22 Third-Party Ladder Assists and Their Limits
03:17 Who Hires a Public Adjuster?
03:35 Public Adjuster Fees and Payment Structures
03:58 When to Bring In a Public Adjuster
04:51 Letters of Representation and Communication Changes
05:23 Risks of Hiring a Public Adjuster Too Early
06:27 Key Takeaways: Helping Homeowners Understand Their Options

REMEMBER WHEN ROOFING WAS SIMPLE?

Gladstone is the AI-powered inbox built for roofing reps handling insurance restoration claims. It helps draft adjuster emails, compare estimates, and prepare supplement communications in your voice.

You review it. You send it. Done.

The second job, handled.

Learn more: https://gladstone-ai.com

Connect with Chris
Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/profile.php?id=61586190076235

Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/gladstone.ai/

Disclaimer

Chris Zimmerman is a roofing contractor, not a licensed public adjuster, insurance agent, or attorney. The questions and communication strategies discussed in this video are examples of how a contractor can ask an insurance adjuster to complete their own investigation and explain their own decisions they are not interpretations of policy language, coverage determinations, or claims advocacy performed on a homeowner's behalf.

Nothing in this video constitutes public adjusting services, insurance advice, or legal advice, and no attorney-client or public-adjuster relationship is formed by watching this content. What any specific policy owes for, covers, or excludes depends on its exact language and the facts of the individual claim. Homeowners with questions about their coverage should consult their insurance carrier, a licensed public adjuster, or an attorney. Contractors are responsible for ensuring their own communications with adjusters and homeowners comply with their state's licensing laws regarding the unauthorized practice of public adjusting.

metadata.title: Restoration Company vs General Contractor: What's the Difference?
metadata.author: PushLeads
metadata.shortDescription:
This video explains the difference between a restoration company and a general contractor, who does what, in what order, and why getting the sequence wrong can cost you thousands and sink your insurance claim. It is for homeowners dealing with water, mold, fire, or storm damage who are trying to figure out who to call first.

Most people assume these two types of companies are interchangeable or competing. They are not. They handle completely different phases of property recovery, use completely different equipment, and the restoration company must always come first when active moisture, contamination, or smoke is involved. I walk through the full picture here so you can make the right call before you sign anything.

- Restoration companies handle emergency mitigation, structural drying, moisture documentation, and contamination removal before any rebuild begins
- General contractors handle reconstruction only after the structure is clean, dry, and documented by the restoration company
- Hiring a GC first with no drying equipment on site can lead to mold inside new walls, a remediation bill, and a denied insurance claim
- Full-service restoration companies that handle both phases under one roof offer real advantages, but ask whether reconstruction is done by in-house employees or subcontractors
- Five specialty services, including structural drying, HEPA mold containment, smoke odor removal, content restoration, and post-remediation verification, are outside a general contractor's training and tool set entirely
- Get both companies and your insurance adjuster communicating from day one, and request the final moisture verification report before the restoration company leaves the job
