segments.text: After property damage, most homeowners ask the same question, do I need a
restoration company,
a general contractor, or both?
These two types of companies do completely different jobs,
use different equipment,
and work in different phases of your recovery.
Hiring the wrong one first can delay your project by weeks and add thousands
in costs you should never have paid.
This video breaks down exactly what each company does.
When you need one versus both, and the one sequencing rule that protects your
insurance claim,
a quick word on who I am, I'm Jeremy,
I run PushLeads,
and I built my career on getting homeowners deciding who to hire after disaster,
ranked, and called.
Everything I'm about to show you comes from 20 years of doing,
not theorizing. In this one, we're walking through hiring a GC after flood
damage can delay your claim and cost you thousands.
Here's why.
Here is the core distinction.
A restoration company handles emergency mitigation, stopping active
damage,
drying the structure,
and removing contaminants.
A general contractor handles reconstruction,
putting the property back together after the environment is stabilized.
These are not competing options.
They are sequential phases.
The restoration company always comes first.
For most significant property damage, you will need both.
The equipment gap between these two types of companies is enormous.
Fully outfitting a restoration operation costs up to $200,000.
A single commercial LGR dehumidifier runs $2,000 to $5,000,
and a restoration company deploys several of them on a single job.
Add HEPA air scrubbers,
thermal imaging cameras,
penetrating moisture meters,
and truck mounted extraction units.
A general contractor owns none of this, because none of it is a construction
tool. When a builder tells you they can dry things out, ask what equipment
they are using, the answer matters.
So what does a restoration company actually do?
They extract standing water with truck mounted units.
They set up commercial drying equipment that typically runs three to five days for
standard water losses.
They pull out damaged materials,
wet drywall, saturated insulation,
contaminated carpet before anything is rebuilt.
They take daily moisture readings to document the drying process for your insurance
carrier.
They apply antimicrobial treatments to block mold.
And for mold jobs, they work under IICRCS 520 protocols with containment barriers
and third party verification.
None of these steps belong to a general contractor.
General contractors are excellent at what they do inside their phase.
Once the restoration company hands off a clean, dry,
documented structure,
the GC frames walls,
installs drywall, handles flooring and cabinetry, coordinates, licensed
electricians and plumbers,
and ensures the rebuild meets building code,
their skills or project management,
construction craftsmanship,
and subcontractor coordination.
The moment you ask them to manage moisture or remove contamination, you are outside
their training and their tool set.
Here is what happens when homeowners hire in the wrong order.
A general contractor starts demo and rebuild.
Nobody sets up drying equipment.
Nobody takes moisture readings.
Three months later, mold appears inside the new walls.
The EPA confirms mold colonies established within 24 to 48 hours of initial
wedding.
That means mold can start growing before the contractor even finishes the first
phase of work.
Now you pay to tear out everything they just built, pay to remediate the
mold,
and you may find your insurance carrier denying the mold claim entirely because they
determine it resulted from improper mitigation,
not the original damage event.
According to the Restoration Industry Association, the average residential water
damage claim involves seven to 10 days of mitigation followed by two to four
weeks of reconstruction.
That two phase timeline is the industry standard, and it exists for a reason.
Fire losses take longer because smoke remediation,
odor treatment,
and content cleaning must all finish before a single piece of new drywall goes
up. If reconstruction starts before the smoke scope is complete,
new finishes seal the contamination in rather than removing it.
Not every loss requires both companies.
Small water damage with limited material removal,
say removing drywall in one room and drying it out can often be handled
entirely by the Restoration Company.
Mold remediation jobs that involve removing contaminated materials and treating
surfaces frequently do not need a GC.
A handyman handles the patch and paint, emergency board up after a storm is
purely restoration territory.
No contractor will arrive at two in the morning to tarp your roof.
On the other side, purely structural repairs with zero moisture or contamination
concerns are the general contractor's call from the start.
Full service restoration companies handle both phases under one roof and that
model is growing.
One point of contact,
one accountability structure,
and no gap between mitigation and reconstruction.
Those are real advantages,
especially on large or complicated losses.
The risk is that some full service companies subcontract the reconstruction work,
which means you are effectively still dealing with two separate crews.
As directly before you sign anything, is reconstruction handled by in -house
employees or subcontractors?
That answer changes everything about who is responsible when something goes wrong.
Also compare total project costs,
not just the mitigation invoice.
On the national franchise versus local independent question,
both can do excellent work.
Franchises bring standardized training and established insurance relationships.
But franchise quality varies by individual owner.
A bright light survey from 2023 found that 98% of consumers
use the internet to research local businesses in the past year.
That means a local independent company's review profile is completely visible.
Check Google reviews,
look at volume and recency,
and ask for references from jobs similar to yours and size and damage type.
Evaluate the specific company showing up to your property,
not the brand name on the truck.
There are five categories of specialty restoration service that a general contractor
simply cannot perform.
Structural drying requires psychrometric calculations and real -time moisture data.
It is a science,
not a construction task.
HEPA mold containment requires negative air pressure and certified disposal.
Smoke odor removal using ozone generators.
Hydroxyl machines or thermal fogging requires operator training and knowledge of
material chemistry.
Content restoration,
cleaning furniture,
electronics,
clothing,
and documents require specialized drying chambers.
And poster mediation verification requires a third -party industrial hygienist.
Many general contractors build referral relationships with restoration companies
specifically
because they encounter these requirements on insurance jobs.
When you are working with two separate companies,
structured communication between all parties prevents gaps and cost overruns.
Get both companies and your insurance adjuster talking directly from day one.
The restoration company's moisture logs,
photo evidence,
and removal scope become the starting point for the GC's reconstruction estimate.
Make sure that documentation actually transfers.
Schedule a walkthrough where the restoration company shows the GC exactly what was
done and what was removed.
Keep copies of every moisture log and drying report.
And before the restoration company leaves the job, request the final moisture
verification report.
That document confirms the structure is dry and protects you if mold appears later.
Here is the decision that determines everything.
Does your property have active moisture,
contamination,
or smoke damage?
If yes, the restoration company goes first, always.
The general contractor follows after you have the final drying report in hand.
For most significant insurance claims, you need both.
For small losses with limited material removal,
the restoration company alone may handle it.
For purely structural repairs with no environmental concerns,
a general contractor is the right call from the start.
Get the sequence right and you protect your structure,
your claim,
and your budget.
If you run a restoration company
and want to be the first result homeowners find when they search this question
in your market, PushLeads builds that visibility.
Get a free teardown at the link in the description,

metadata.title: Watch This BEFORE You Do Everything Your Insurance Adjuster Says
metadata.author: Chris Zimmerman
metadata.shortDescription:
Your adjuster just told you to go get a form filled out by the city, submit extra paperwork, or jump through one more hoop before they'll approve your claim. Before you do it wait. Here's the one question that tells you whether that's a real requirement or an adjuster stalling for time.

In this video I break down a real scenario from inside a contractor community: an insurance adjuster demanding extra third-party documentation before approving a legitimate claim. I walk through how to tell the difference between a reasonable request and an adjuster adding requirements they have no authority to add and the simple, disarming question that exposes which one you're dealing with, without ever arguing.

You'll learn:

-The one question that forces an adjuster to clarify: is this a recommendation, or a requirement?
-Why saying yes to one extra ask almost always leads to another ("give a moose a muffin")
-How to push back on an out-of-scope documentation request without playing the insurance claim specialist
-Why staying in your contractor sandbox actually gives you more leverage, not less
-How Gladstone helps you turn this kind of pushback into a homeowner-friendly explanation, not a confrontation
-If you've ever felt like an insurance adjuster was stalling your claim with endless extra requests, this is the mindset shift and the exact language that stops it.

Chapters

0:00 – Wait Before You Do What Your Adjuster Just Told You 
0:48 – Is This Adjuster Acting Outside Their Authority? 
1:30 – The Question: "Is This a Recommendation or a Requirement?" 2:33 – If You Give a Moose a Muffin: Why One Ask Becomes Ten 
3:25 – "Misapplication of Coverage": Why Roofers Shouldn't Say This 4:23 – The Uno Reverse: Putting the Burden Back on the Adjuster 
6:50 – How Gladstone Helps You Explain This to Your Homeowner 
8:56 – Subscribe for Weekly Adjuster Strategy

Check out GLADSTONE:
https://gladstone-ai.com/

Connect with Chris
Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/profile.php?id=61586190076235

Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/gladstone.ai/

Disclaimer

Chris Zimmerman is a roofing contractor, not a licensed public adjuster, insurance agent, or attorney. The questions and communication strategies discussed in this video are examples of how a contractor can ask an insurance adjuster to complete their own investigation and explain their own decisions they are not interpretations of policy language, coverage determinations, or claims advocacy performed on a homeowner's behalf.

Nothing in this video constitutes public adjusting services, insurance advice, or legal advice, and no attorney-client or public-adjuster relationship is formed by watching this content. What any specific policy owes for, covers, or excludes depends on its exact language and the facts of the individual claim. Homeowners with questions about their coverage should consult their insurance carrier, a licensed public adjuster, or an attorney. Contractors are responsible for ensuring their own communications with adjusters and homeowners comply with their state's licensing laws regarding the unauthorized practice of public adjusting.

#InsuranceAdjuster #InsuranceClaim #RoofingContractor #InsuranceClaimDenied #InsuranceRestoration #RoofingSales

metadata.title: What Does a Public Adjuster Actually Do? Insurance Estimates, Settlements & Your Rights
metadata.author: claimhelpme
metadata.shortDescription:
Hiring a public adjuster doesn't guarantee you're hiring someone who understands construction, insurance estimating, repair costs, or how to defend a disputed property damage claim.

Who actually writes your estimate? Who challenges the insurance company's numbers? And who explains what you're giving up before accepting a settlement?

This video examines a real property insurance claim involving approximately $112,000 in documented repair and contents-handling scope that ultimately settled for approximately $40,000.

The homeowner was satisfied. But did they fully understand the unresolved repair costs?

Public adjusting involves more than submitting paperwork. It requires understanding the damage, documenting the scope, reviewing insurance estimates, addressing disputed costs, and explaining settlement decisions.

15 QUESTIONS HOMEOWNERS SHOULD ASK ABOUT PUBLIC ADJUSTERS:

1. What does a public adjuster actually do?
2. Who prepares your insurance repair estimate?
3. Does your public adjuster understand construction?
4. What happens when an insurance estimate is too low?
5. Who negotiates disputed repair costs?
6. Why are flooring and cabinetry sometimes excluded?
7. What is an insurance claim supplement?
8. Can you accept an undisputed payment without settling?
9. What happens when you accept a low settlement?
10. How does recoverable depreciation work?
11. What should a public adjuster explain before settlement?
12. How long do claims remain on a C.L.U.E. report?
13. Can an insurance claim affect future premiums?
14. What should you ask before hiring a public adjuster?
15. How do you know your claim is properly represented?

A public adjuster license doesn't automatically establish construction or estimating expertise.

Some adjusters prepare their own estimates. Others outsource the work. What matters is whether your representative can verify the scope, defend legitimate charges, and explain the consequences of accepting a settlement.

GOOD ENOUGH FOR WHOM?

The insurance company? The public adjuster? Or the homeowner who still has to repair the property?

ClaimHelpMe provides free property insurance education, estimating guidance, documentation standards, and real-world claim case studies.

SCOPE IT. DOCUMENT IT. SUPPORT IT.

Free information. No subscription. No obligation to hire anyone.

metadata.title: Ask Avner Deep Dive: Restoration Companies vs Insurance Claims
metadata.author: Avner Gat, Inc. - Public Insurance Adjusters
metadata.shortDescription:
What’s the biggest mistake homeowners make after water or fire damage?
Letting restoration companies handle insurance claim negotiations instead of a licensed public adjuster.

In this Ask Avner Deep Dive episode, Avner Gat, a licensed public insurance adjuster in California, explains what homeowners often don’t know after a water damage or fire damage claim. Many restoration companies are hired to dry a home, but they are not licensed to negotiate insurance settlements or manage the full scope of an insurance claim.

Avner breaks down:
- What restoration companies are legally supposed to do after water damage
- Why asbestos and lead testing must happen before demolition
- When asbestos abatement is required
- Why insurance claim negotiation requires a public adjuster license
- How letting contractors negotiate with insurance can delay or damage a claim
- The hidden parts of a claim, including temporary housing, personal property, storage, and repair scope
- Why insurance companies may see a conflict of interest when restoration companies negotiate and repair

This video is for homeowners and property owners dealing with insurance claims who want to avoid costly mistakes and understand who should handle each part of the claims process.

I’m Avner Gat, a licensed public adjuster, helping homeowners and business owners across California navigate insurance claims with clarity and confidence.

metadata.title: How to Get More Out of Your First Insurance Adjuster Meeting
metadata.author: Chris Zimmerman
metadata.shortDescription:
Meeting an insurance adjuster for the first time? What you bring, what you say, and how you handle the roof inspection can make or break your credibility.

In this video, I walk through how roofing contractors and sales reps should prepare for an insurance adjuster meeting during a roof insurance claim.

Whether you're dealing with hail damage, wind damage, or another storm damage insurance claim, the adjuster appointment is an important opportunity to present your findings, provide documentation, and make sure the damage you've identified gets reviewed.

But there's a right way and a wrong way to approach it.

I've seen roofing reps show up without basic tools, argue with adjusters on the roof, make definitive statements they can't support, and leave without getting everyone on the same page.

Those mistakes can create unnecessary problems for the homeowner and the claim.

I'll explain what I recommend bringing to an insurance adjuster inspection, how to walk the roof professionally, the questions I'd ask during the appointment, and why the conversation after the inspection is just as important as the inspection itself.

The goal isn't to argue with the adjuster. It's to build credibility, communicate with facts, and make sure the homeowner understands what happened.

IN THIS VIDEO:

-What to bring to an insurance adjuster meeting
-Why your ladder, tools, photos, and detailed estimate matter
-How to walk the roof with an insurance adjuster
-Questions to ask before and during the roof inspection
-What roofing contractors should and shouldn't say
-Why making unsupported claims about hail or wind damage can hurt your credibility
-How to recap the inspection with the homeowner and adjuster
-Why documenting conversations can help avoid misunderstandings
How recording tools can help with meeting notes and follow-up

VIDEO CHAPTERS

0:00 Introduction
0:33 What to Bring to the Meeting
1:46 Walking the Roof with the Adjuster
3:36 What to Say and Not to Say
4:15 The Recap After the Meeting
6:57 Recording the Conversation

RECORDING YOUR ADJUSTER MEETINGS

One tool I've found helpful is Plaud. It can record conversations, transcribe them, and summarize important information so you have a better record of what was discussed.

Use code CHRIS5 for 5% off if you decide to purchase one.

Make sure you understand the recording and consent laws that apply where you're working before recording any conversation.

Check out GLADSTONE:
https://gladstone-ai.com/

Connect with Chris
Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/profile.php?id=61586190076235

Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/gladstone.ai/

Disclaimer

Chris Zimmerman is a roofing contractor, not a licensed public adjuster, insurance agent, or attorney. The questions and communication strategies discussed in this video are examples of how a contractor can ask an insurance adjuster to complete their own investigation and explain their own decisions they are not interpretations of policy language, coverage determinations, or claims advocacy performed on a homeowner's behalf.

Nothing in this video constitutes public adjusting services, insurance advice, or legal advice, and no attorney-client or public-adjuster relationship is formed by watching this content. What any specific policy owes for, covers, or excludes depends on its exact language and the facts of the individual claim. Homeowners with questions about their coverage should consult their insurance carrier, a licensed public adjuster, or an attorney. Contractors are responsible for ensuring their own communications with adjusters and homeowners comply with their state's licensing laws regarding the unauthorized practice of public adjusting.

metadata.title: 7 Levels of Public Adjusters: Simple Claims to Total Chaos
metadata.author: American Roof Supplements
metadata.shortDescription:
👉 Your first Xactimate estimate or supplement is FREE. Book a 10-minute setup call with Joe: https://bit.ly/ARS-FreeSupplement
No monthly fees, no minimums. Pay per job: $50 per estimate, $150 per supplement.

What does a public adjuster actually do—and what happens when a simple roof insurance claim turns into a complicated dispute?

One storm. One damaged roof. Three different estimates. And suddenly, everyone has a different opinion about what should happen next.

In this video, we break down **7 levels of public adjusting**, from the first homeowner phone call to complex insurance claims, disputed roofing estimates, hidden damage, and major catastrophe losses.

You'll learn:

- What a licensed public adjuster does—and how that role differs from a roofing contractor or insurance company adjuster.
- Why roof inspections, accurate measurements, and damage documentation matter.
- How Xactimate estimates and supplements fit into the claim process.
- Why missing line items, decking damage, flashing, and code-related work require proper support.
- Where roofing contractors must be careful not to cross into public adjusting.
- How claim complexity increases—and when specialized professionals may be needed.

**For roofing contractors and licensed public adjusters:**

American Roof Supplements provides residential Xactimate estimates, supplements, and supporting construction documentation.

We help organize legitimate roofing scope, measurements, photos, material information, and construction-related details for carrier review.

Licensed public adjusters receive the same pricing as roofing contractors. There are no monthly fees or minimum job requirements.

Your first estimate or supplement is free. After that, residential pre-adjuster estimates are $50, standalone supplements are $150, and qualifying follow-up supplements are $100 when ARS prepared the estimate for that same approved job.

American Roof Supplements is not a public-adjusting company or law firm. We do not determine insurance coverage, interpret policies, negotiate claims, or guarantee approvals. Those responsibilities remain with the appropriate licensed professionals and the insurer.

Whether you're a roofing contractor trying to understand the insurance claim process or a licensed public adjuster looking for technical estimating support, this video explains why good documentation matters at every level.

**Which level creates the biggest headaches in your experience?** Let us know in the comments.

Share this video with your roofing crew, fellow public adjusters, or anyone working with property insurance claims.

Subscribe for more practical roofing, Xactimate, supplement, and claim-documentation content.

#PublicAdjuster #RoofingContractor #InsuranceClaims #Xactimate #RoofingSupplements

segments.text: Picture this. Monday morning, a roofing
contractor gets a call about a few
missing shingles. Easy inspection,
right? By Thursday, half the roof is
open. The crew has found deteriorated
decking. Rain is moving in, and the
carrier's estimate doesn't match what's
actually on the house. The homeowner
wants answers, and the public adjuster
faces a complicated claim. Here's the
real question. When a claim goes from
routine to chaos, who handles what, and
who has the authority to do it? Today,
we're breaking down seven levels of
public adjusting, from that first phone
call to major catastrophe claims. Level
four is the real stress test, and level
seven is where even experienced
professionals need to know when to bring
in help. Before we climb, let's get the
roles straight. A staff adjuster works
for an insurance company. An independent
adjuster may be hired by an insurer. A
licensed public adjuster represents the
policy holder in the claim process,
subject to state law. A roofing
contractor evaluates and performs
construction work. Those professionals
can share evidence and coordinate, but
their responsibilities aren't
interchangeable. If you're a roofer,
understanding that boundary protects
your business. If you're a public
adjuster, understanding the contractor's
technical role makes your file stronger.
Level one, the intake. A homeowner calls
after a hailstorm. The roof looks rough.
A neighbor already filed a claim, and
somebody on social media says every
house on the block needs replacement.
That's not an investigation. That's
neighborhood gossip with a deductible. A
careful public adjuster starts with the
facts. Property details, reported loss
date, prior repairs, existing
photographs, the carrier's involvement,
and what the policy holder actually
needs.
Before accepting representation, the
adjuster checks licensing, contract
requirements, disclosures, and any
applicable solicitation or cancellation
rules. Those details vary by state,
especially around catastrophes. For
contractors, the lesson is equally
practical. Document the condition and
communicate your construction findings.
Don't assume a roofing contract
authorizes you to represent the insured
in a claim. Not every claim needs a
public adjuster, but complicated
disputes may.
Level two, the inspection. Now the crew
is on the roof and opinions have to give
way to evidence. A dark spot isn't
automatically hail damage. A ceiling
stain doesn't identify the entry point
and one missing shingle doesn't prove an
entire roof must be replaced. Record
roof dimensions, slopes, materials,
flashing, penetrations, ventilation,
accessories, interior conditions, and
relevant surrounding damage. Photograph
the overall slope before zooming in on
the detail.
Put a measurement beside a questionable
area. Label what you're showing. A
public adjuster may use those
construction findings while evaluating
and presenting the insured's claim
within their legal authority. The
contractor's job is to make the
technical facts clear, not to promise
what the policy will pay.
Imagine water staining near a chimney. A
weak file says, "Leak at chimney." and
includes one blurry picture. A stronger
file documents step flashing, counter
flashing, the roof to wall connection,
nearby shingles, and the visible
moisture path. It also records what
remains uncertain. That's the difference
between a conclusion and an
investigation. Good professionals don't
force every photograph to tell the story
they wanted. They let the conditions
lead. Level three, the estimate. The
carrier lists one set of operations. The
contractor's scope lists another. The
public adjuster is working through the
claim and now three people are looking
at numbers that don't agree. Here's the
mistake, treating the largest total as
the best estimate. The real questions
are about quantities and construction.
Do measurements match? Are the correct
materials identified? Are starter, ridge
cap, flashing, vents, tear-off,
disposal, and access conditions included
where justified? Can each disputed
operation be tied to the actual roof?
Xactimate helps organize line items,
quantities, and pricing. It does not
decide insurance coverage. A beautifully
formatted estimate can still contain
unsupported work. A short estimate can
still miss legitimate operations. So,
strip away the dollar signs for a
second. Can you explain the difference
using measurements, photographs,
manufacturer information, or field
notes? If not, don't start with a louder
argument. Start with a better file. This
is also where technical estimating
support can help roofing contractors and
licensed public adjusters organize
legitimate scope without crossing into
claim representation. Level four, the
roof is open. Here's where our easy
Monday inspection goes sideways. The
crew removes shingles and find soft
decking in multiple sections. A second
area looks worse. A thunderstorm is
approaching. The homeowner is calling
every 10 minutes. The carrier's original
estimate doesn't address what the crew
just uncovered. Everybody wants an
immediate answer, but rushing the
paperwork won't make the roof
watertight. First, address safety and
temporary protection. Then, capture the
conditions before they're covered or
discarded. Record locations, dimensions,
materials, photographs, and the
construction reason a particular
operation may be necessary. Preserve
supporting manufacturer instructions or
locally adopted code references where
applicable.
Coordinate the technical findings with
the licensed professional responsible
for claim representation.
And this is the point that separates
serious documentation from wishful
thinking.
Finding deteriorated decking does not
automatically mean the insurer owes for
it. Neither does quoting a code section.
Construction necessity, code
applicability, causation, and insurance
coverage are related questions, but
they're not the same question. A
contractor can explain what it takes to
build the roof correctly. A licensed
public adjuster can address the
insured's claim within their permitted
scope. If the issue turns legal, an
attorney may be needed. Clear roles keep
a stressful situation from becoming a
bigger mess.
Level five, the disagreement. The
documentation is solid. The carrier
still doesn't agree with part of the
requested scope. This is where a strong
contractor and a licensed public
adjuster can complement each other. The
contractor explains installation
methods, materials, measurements, and
why the work is necessary. The public
adjuster handles the claim advocacy and
representation that state law permits.
Both need accurate information.
Neither benefits from inflated line
items, missing evidence, or promises of
guaranteed payment.
There are important state-specific
boundaries. In Texas, for example,
regulators warn roofing contractors
against acting as public adjusters on
properties where they provide or may
provide roofing services. Contractors
can still supply estimates and technical
construction information within
applicable rules, but don't assume one
state's framework applies nationwide.
Check the law where the property is
located and don't confuse explaining a
roof with negotiating an insurance
settlement.
Level six, the loss spreads. Water may
have reached insulation, drywall, or
electrical systems. Maybe multiple
storms complicate the timeline. Maybe an
engineer needs to examine causation, or
a mitigation company has records the
team hasn't seen. A skilled public
adjuster knows how to coordinate the
claim work they're licensed to perform,
while contractors and specialists
document their own findings. The best
file separates observed facts,
professional opinions, and unanswered
questions. That distinction matters when
different people remember the same storm
differently. Sometimes the dispute moves
beyond construction quantities into
policy language or legal rights.
Appraisal may be available for certain
valuation disputes under some policies,
but it isn't a universal answer to
coverage disagreements. A public
adjuster license is not a law degree.
Knowing when an attorney or another
specialist should step in is part of
protecting the client and the integrity
of the file.
Level seven, catastrophe mode. A major
storm hits multiple counties. Schedules
fill up. Contractors are working long
days and public adjusters are juggling
complex files under serious time
pressure. Suddenly, licensing across
state lines, emergency rules,
solicitation restrictions, fee limits,
contract disclosures, and record keeping
all matter at once. Nobody gets a free
pass because the storm was big. A strong
operation knows who is authorized to
act, keeps documentation consistent, and
makes sure the insured understands who
represents them.
At this level, the professionals who
stand out aren't necessarily the
loudest. They're the ones who can open a
file six months later and explain every
important decision. The photographs
match the measurements. The scope
matches the actual conditions. The
revisions are traceable. The contractor
speaks to construction. The public
adjuster speaks within the scope of
licensed representation. And when
something falls outside either person's
expertise, they bring in the right
professional.
That brings us to American Roof
Supplements. For roofing contractors and
licensed public adjusters, a
well-organized technical file can save
time and reduce confusion. Our role is
supporting legitimate construction
estimating and documentation, not
stepping into the public adjuster's
shoes. Here's exactly what we do, how
pricing works, and how to get started.
American Roof Supplements prepares
residential Xactimate estimates,
supplements, and supporting
documentation. We document legitimate
construction scope with measurements,
photos, product information, notes, and
supported construction or code-related
operations.
American Roof Supplements is not a
public adjusting company or law firm.
Supplements do not create coverage,
change the deductible, turn actual cash
value coverage into replacement cost
coverage, make non-recoverable
depreciation recoverable, or guarantee
approval. The carrier determines
coverage, policy interpretation, claim
negotiation, public adjusting, and legal
representation stay with the appropriate
licensed professional. We help roofing
contractors with residential Xactimate
estimates, supplements, and supporting
documentation. When a carrier estimate
may be missing legitimate scope, we
organize the supporting construction
documentation for carrier review. Your
first estimate or supplement is free.
After that, a pre-adjuster residential
Xactimate estimate is $50. If we
prepared the estimate for that same job
and the job is approved, the follow-up
supplement is $100. A standalone
supplement is $150.
There is no monthly fee, no minimum
number of jobs, and you pay per job.
Licensed public adjusters pay the same
prices as everyone else. Property
insurance attorneys can contact us for
Xactimate estimating or technical
construction documentation. Reasonable
revisions are included. Use the link at
the top of the description to book a
10-minute setup call with Joe, or call
or text American Roof Supplements at
Newer roofing contractors receive extra
guidance through their first five
claims, including help preparing for
carrier conversations. Those first five
claims are an onboarding benefit, not a
cutoff. Support continues afterward.
If this helped, share it with your
roofing team, roofing Facebook group,
WhatsApp group, or another professional
who could use it.
Subscribe for more practical roofing,
Xactimate, supplement, and claim
documentation content.
Because here's the truth about all seven
levels. The claim doesn't become easier
when everyone talks louder. It becomes
clearer when the evidence gets better,
and the right professional handles the
right job. From one missing shingle to a
roof full of surprises, that's the
standard worth building your reputation
on.

Those details vary by state, especially around catastrophes. For contractors, the lesson is equally practical. Document the condition and communicate your construction findings. Don't assume a roofing contract authorizes you to represent the insured in a claim. Not every claim needs a public adjuster, but complicated disputes may. Level two, the inspection. Now the crew is on the roof and opinions have to give way to evidence. A dark spot isn't automatically hail damage. A ceiling stain doesn't identify the entry point and one missing shingle doesn't prove an entire roof must be replaced. Record roof dimensions, slopes, materials, flashing, penetrations, ventilation, accessories, interior conditions, and relevant surrounding damage. Photograph the overall slope before zooming in on the detail. Put a measurement beside a questionable area. Label what you're showing. A public adjuster may use those construction findings while evaluating and presenting the insured's claim within their legal authority. The contractor's job is to make the technical facts clear, not to promise what the policy will pay. Imagine water staining near a chimney. A weak file says, "Leak at chimney." and includes one blurry picture. A stronger file documents step flashing, counter flashing, the roof to wall connection, nearby shingles, and the visible moisture path. It also records what remains uncertain. That's the difference between a conclusion and an investigation. Good professionals don't force every photograph to tell the story they wanted. They let the conditions lead. Level three, the estimate. The carrier lists one set of operations. The contractor's scope lists another. The public adjuster is working through the claim and now three people are looking at numbers that don't agree. Here's the mistake, treating the largest total as the best estimate. The real questions are about quantities and construction. Do measurements match? Are the correct materials identified? Are starter, ridge cap, flashing, vents, tear-off, disposal, and access conditions included where justified? Can each disputed operation be tied to the actual roof? Xactimate helps organize line items, quantities, and pricing. It does not decide insurance coverage. A beautifully formatted estimate can still contain unsupported work. A short estimate can still miss legitimate operations. So, strip away the dollar signs for a second. Can you explain the difference using measurements, photographs, manufacturer information, or field notes? If not, don't start with a louder argument. Start with a better file. This is also where technical estimating support can help roofing contractors and licensed public adjusters organize legitimate scope without crossing into claim representation. Level four, the roof is open. Here's where our easy Monday inspection goes sideways. The crew removes shingles and find soft decking in multiple sections. A second area looks worse. A thunderstorm is approaching. The homeowner is calling every 10 minutes. The carrier's original estimate doesn't address what the crew just uncovered. Everybody wants an immediate answer, but rushing the paperwork won't make the roof watertight. First, address safety and temporary protection. Then, capture the conditions before they're covered or discarded. Record locations, dimensions, materials, photographs, and the construction reason a particular operation may be necessary. Preserve supporting manufacturer instructions or locally adopted code references where applicable. Coordinate the technical findings with the licensed professional responsible for claim representation. And this is the point that separates serious documentation from wishful thinking. Finding deteriorated decking does not automatically mean the insurer owes for it. Neither does quoting a code section. Construction necessity, code applicability, causation, and insurance coverage are related questions, but they're not the same question. A contractor can explain what it takes to build the roof correctly. A licensed public adjuster can address the insured's claim within their permitted scope. If the issue turns legal, an attorney may be needed. Clear roles keep a stressful situation from becoming a bigger mess. Level five, the disagreement. The documentation is solid. The carrier still doesn't agree with part of the requested scope. This is where a strong contractor and a licensed public adjuster can complement each other. The contractor explains installation methods, materials, measurements, and why the work is necessary. The public adjuster handles the claim advocacy and representation that state law permits. Both need accurate information. Neither benefits from inflated line items, missing evidence, or promises of guaranteed payment. There are important state-specific boundaries. In Texas, for example, regulators warn roofing contractors against acting as public adjusters on properties where they provide or may provide roofing services. Contractors can still supply estimates and technical construction information within applicable rules, but don't assume one state's framework applies nationwide. Check the law where the property is located and don't confuse explaining a roof with negotiating an insurance settlement. Level six, the loss spreads. Water may have reached insulation, drywall, or electrical systems. Maybe multiple storms complicate the timeline. Maybe an engineer needs to examine causation, or a mitigation company has records the team hasn't seen. A skilled public adjuster knows how to coordinate the claim work they're licensed to perform, while contractors and specialists document their own findings. The best file separates observed facts, professional opinions, and unanswered questions. That distinction matters when different people remember the same storm differently. Sometimes the dispute moves beyond construction quantities into policy language or legal rights. Appraisal may be available for certain valuation disputes under some policies, but it isn't a universal answer to coverage disagreements. A public adjuster license is not a law degree. Knowing when an attorney or another specialist should step in is part of protecting the client and the integrity of the file. Level seven, catastrophe mode. A major storm hits multiple counties. Schedules fill up. Contractors are working long days and public adjusters are juggling complex files under serious time pressure. Suddenly, licensing across state lines, emergency rules, solicitation restrictions, fee limits, contract disclosures, and record keeping all matter at once. Nobody gets a free pass because the storm was big. A strong operation knows who is authorized to act, keeps documentation consistent, and makes sure the insured understands who represents them. At this level, the professionals who stand out aren't necessarily the loudest. They're the ones who can open a file six months later and explain every important decision. The photographs match the measurements. The scope matches the actual conditions. The revisions are traceable. The contractor speaks to construction. The public adjuster speaks within the scope of licensed representation. And when something falls outside either person's expertise, they bring in the right professional. That brings us to American Roof Supplements. For roofing contractors and licensed public adjusters, a well-organized technical file can save time and reduce confusion. Our role is supporting legitimate construction estimating and documentation, not stepping into the public adjuster's shoes. Here's exactly what we do, how pricing works, and how to get started. American Roof Supplements prepares residential Xactimate estimates, supplements, and supporting documentation. We document legitimate construction scope with measurements, photos, product information, notes, and supported construction or code-related operations. American Roof Supplements is not a public adjusting company or law firm. Supplements do not create coverage, change the deductible, turn actual cash value coverage into replacement cost coverage, make non-recoverable depreciation recoverable, or guarantee approval. The carrier determines coverage, policy interpretation, claim negotiation, public adjusting, and legal representation stay with the appropriate licensed professional. We help roofing contractors with residential Xactimate estimates, supplements, and supporting documentation. When a carrier estimate may be missing legitimate scope, we organize the supporting construction documentation for carrier review. Your first estimate or supplement is free. After that, a pre-adjuster residential Xactimate estimate is $50. If we prepared the estimate for that same job and the job is approved, the follow-up supplement is $100. A standalone supplement is $150. There is no monthly fee, no minimum number of jobs, and you pay per job. Licensed public adjusters pay the same prices as everyone else. Property insurance attorneys can contact us for Xactimate estimating or technical construction documentation. Reasonable revisions are included. Use the link at the top of the description to book a 10-minute setup call with Joe, or call or text American Roof Supplements at 469-515-8435. Newer roofing contractors receive extra guidance through their first five claims, including help preparing for carrier conversations. Those first five claims are an onboarding benefit, not a cutoff. Support continues afterward. If this helped, share it with your roofing team, roofing Facebook group, WhatsApp group, or another professional who could use it. Subscribe for more practical roofing, Xactimate, supplement, and claim documentation content. Because here's the truth about all seven levels. The claim doesn't become easier when everyone talks louder. It becomes clearer when the evidence gets better, and the right professional handles the right job. From one missing shingle to a roof full of surprises, that's the standard worth building your reputation on.

metadata.title: He Signed One Form at His Front Door and Lost Control of His Own Claim | Assignment of Benefits
metadata.author: The Fine Print
metadata.shortDescription:
A composite homeowner story drawn from documented patterns in Assignment of Benefits abuse, primarily in Florida, where contractors took over insurance claims, inflated repair invoices, and sued insurers in the homeowner's name. Based on Florida Office of Insurance Regulation findings, the 2019 AOB reform law, and reporting on roofing and water-mitigation AOB litigation.

Key references:
- Florida Office of Insurance Regulation data on AOB lawsuit growth (2013-2018)
- Florida House Bill 7065 (2019), AOB reform legislation
- Florida Department of Financial Services consumer warnings on AOB door-to-door solicitation

Educational content only. Insurance products vary by state and situation — consult a licensed agent before purchasing. The homeowner is a composite; the documented patterns and cited law are matters of public record.

#Insurance #HomeInsurance #AssignmentOfBenefits #HomeownerRights #TheFinePrint

Chapters:
0:00 The Knock After The Storm
0:31 What He Actually Signed
1:02 From $8,000 To $22,000
1:30 The Lawsuit In His Name
2:00 The Lawsuit Is The Business
2:29 A Statewide Crisis
2:56 Then The Non-Renewal
3:22 Not Simple To Unwind
3:49 Protect Yourself First
4:23 Worth More Than The Shingles
4:50 Next Episode

segments.text: The knock came 2 days after the storm. A
man in a branded polo, clipboard in
hand, said he had noticed damage to the
roof from the street. He could get it
fixed at no cost out of pocket.
The insurance would cover everything.
All the homeowner had to do was sign one
form so the company could deal directly
with the insurer. It was, the man said,
just paperwork.
The homeowner signed it on the porch, on
the clipboard, without reading the back.
That signature did not start a repair.
It signed away control of his entire
claim.
The form was an assignment of benefits.
In plain terms, [music]
it transfers your right to your
insurance claim to a third party,
usually a contractor. Once you sign it,
the contractor steps into your shoes.
They negotiate with your insurer. They
submit the invoices. They decide what
the repair costs. And, critically, they
gain the right to sue your insurance
company over the claim, not you.
Them. Using your policy.
The homeowner thought he was authorizing
a repair. He was authorizing a stranger
to litigate in his name.
For a while, nothing seemed wrong. The
crew arrived, tarped the roof, and began
work.
>> [music]
>> Then the invoices flowed to the insurer.
The first estimate had been around
The submitted invoice came in at 22,000
with line items the homeowner had never
seen. Water mitigation he did not
remember happening. Materials in
quantities that did not match his roof.
He had no easy way to question it. He
had assigned away his standing. The
claim was no longer his to manage. The
insurer pushed back and disputed the
inflated invoice. Under a normal claim,
the homeowner and the insurer would
negotiate.
Under the assignment, that negotiation
now happened between the contractor and
the insurer, with the homeowner as a
bystander. And when the insurer refused
to pay the full 22,000, the contractor
did exactly what the form allowed. It
filed a lawsuit against the insurance
company, naming the homeowner's policy,
seeking the disputed amount plus
attorney fees. Why would a contractor
want to sue? The answer is in the fee
structure. For years, in states like
Florida, the law awarded attorney fees
to the claimant side in insurance
disputes in a way that favored whoever
held the claim.
A contractor who sued and won, even over
a small disputed amount, could recover
large legal fees from the insurer. The
repair was almost beside the point. The
lawsuit itself became the business
model.
File enough of them and the fees add up
faster than the roofing. The scale
became a crisis. Florida regulators
documented an explosion in AOB lawsuits
over the 2010s, from a few thousand a
year to tens of thousands. Each one
carried legal costs.
Insurers passed those costs back to your
premiums. Homeowners across the state,
most of whom never signed an assignment,
paid higher rates because of lawsuits
filed in other homeowners' names. The
single porch signature, multiplied
across a market, became a line item on
everyone's bill.
The homeowner's troubles were not only
the contractors. The lawsuit, filed in
his policy's name, became part of his
claims history.
When his policy came up for renewal, the
insurer declined to renew.
A claim with active litigation attached
makes a homeowner harder to insure. He
had not sued anyone. He had not wanted a
lawsuit.
But the record showed a contested claim
on his property, and the next insurer he
approached saw exactly that.
>> [music]
>> He tried to revoke the assignment and
learned it was not simple. Once signed
and acted upon, an assignment is a
contract. The contractor had begun work
and incurred costs.
Walking it back meant a dispute with the
contractor on top of the dispute with
the insurer.
He hired his own lawyer, finally, and
discovered that the form he signed in 30
seconds would take months and legal fees
to unwind.
The cheapest decision of his week had
become the most expensive of his year.
States have moved to curb the worst of
it.
>> [music]
>> Florida passed a major AOB reform law in
2019, House Bill 7065, that reshaped the
fee structure, required assignment forms
to carry specific disclosures, and gave
homeowners a window to rescind. So,
protect yourself before someone knocks.
Never sign anything at the door. Call
your insurer and report the damage
yourself before any signature. Get your
own written estimate first.
>> [music]
>> And if the words assignment of benefits
appear on a form, understand you are
transferring your claim, not authorizing
a repair. He got a new roof. He also got
a lawsuit in his name, a non-renewed
policy, and a year of legal cleanup he
never asked for. The damage to his house
was fixed in a week.
The damage to his standing took far
longer. The man on the porch was not
selling a repair. He was buying a
signature, and the signature was worth
more to him than the shingles.
The fine print on a clipboard is still
fine print. The only difference is that
this time someone was holding the pen
out to you and telling you not to read
it. If this one stayed with you, episode
5 on the insurers fleeing Florida and
California, and what homeowners are left
with, goes further down the same road.
The lawsuit flood you just watched is
one reason those companies walked away.
It is on this channel.

metadata.shortDescription:
In this enlightening episode of the Claims Underground Podcast, we explore the intricacies of Assignment of Benefits (AOB) with the help of top public adjusters. AOB is an essential but often misunderstood aspect of insurance claims, and having a thorough understanding of its implications is crucial for both insurance professionals and policyholders. This episode demystifies AOB, providing valuable insights, expert advice, and real-life examples to help you master this vital element of the claims process.

💡 What to expect from this episode:

An in-depth explanation of the Assignment of Benefits and its role in insurance claims.

The pros and cons of AOB for policyholders, contractors, and insurance professionals.

Expert tips and strategies for handling AOB agreements effectively and ethically.

Common misconceptions and pitfalls associated with AOB.

Real-life stories and experiences from top public adjusters dealing with AOB scenarios.

Understanding and mastering the Assignment of Benefits is crucial for navigating the complex world of insurance claims. This episode of the Claims Underground Podcast equips you with the knowledge and tools needed to handle AOB agreements with confidence and expertise, ensuring the best possible outcomes for all parties involved.

👍 If you found this episode informative and engaging, please like, subscribe, and share it with your colleagues, friends, and fellow insurance enthusiasts. Be sure to hit the notification bell to stay informed about all our latest content, featuring expert discussions and advice on a wide range of insurance topics and industry trends.

💬 We'd love to hear your thoughts, experiences, and questions related to the Assignment of Benefits and the claims process. Please share them in the comments section below. Your feedback helps us create content that is relevant and valuable to our community of insurance professionals and interested individuals.

#ClaimsUndergroundPodcast #AssignmentOfBenefits #TopPublicAdjustersInsights

metadata.title: What Is an Assignment of Benefits (AOB)? | Should You Sign One After a Property Damage Claim?
metadata.author: Happy Adjuster
metadata.shortDescription:
If you’re dealing with water damage, roof damage, or mold — chances are, a contractor might ask you to sign something called an Assignment of Benefits (AOB). But what exactly is it? And should you sign it?

In this video, we break down:
✅ What an Assignment of Benefits is
✅ Why contractors use it in insurance claims
✅ The risks homeowners should watch out for
✅ When signing one might make sense — and when to think twice

At Happy Adjuster, we believe informed homeowners make better decisions. And we’re here to help you avoid costly mistakes when navigating your claim.

📞 Need help reviewing documents before you sign? Book a virtual consultation:
👉 http://www.happyadjuster.pro

segments.text: If a contractor asks you to sign
something called an assignment of
benefits or AOB, consider this before
you grab a pen. An assignment of
benefits AOB is a legal agreement that
allows a third party, usually a
contractor, roofer, or restoration
company, to take over your insurance
claim on your behalf. When you sign an
AOB, you're giving that company the
right to deal directly with your
insurance company, file paperwork, and
even receive payment from the claim
without needing your approval. It might
sound convenient, especially when you're
stressed and just want the repairs
handled. But it's important to
understand exactly what you're agreeing
to. While some contractors use AOS
responsibly, others use them to take
control of the claim and may charge for
work that's overpriced, unnecessary, or
even never completed. Once you've signed
an AOB, you could be cut out of the
conversation entirely. And in some
cases, you may end up in the middle of a
legal dispute between the contractor and
your insurance company. Let's start with
the pros. Convenience. An AOB means you
won't have to deal directly with the
insurance company. The contractor takes
care of it for you. Faster repairs. Some
contractors will get started right away,
even while the claim is still being
processed. Professional handling. And
some experienced vendors really do know
how to navigate insurance paperwork,
which can be a headache. Now, here's
where you need to be careful. The cons.
Loss of control. Once you sign, the
contractor can make decisions about the
claim without checking in with you.
Inflated charges. If they overcharge and
your insurer refuses to pay the full
bill, guess who's stuck with the
difference? You. Legal issues. In some
cases, AOS have led to lawsuits and the
homeowner got pulled right into the
middle of it. Quality concerns. And if
the contractor gets paid upfront, some
might cut corners or even disappear
altogether.

An assignment of benefits AOB is a legal agreement that allows a third party, usually a contractor, roofer, or restoration company, to take over your insurance claim on your behalf. When you sign an AOB, you're giving that company the right to deal directly with your insurance company, file paperwork, and even receive payment from the claim without needing your approval. It might sound convenient, especially when you're stressed and just want the repairs handled. But it's important to understand exactly what you're agreeing to. While some contractors use AOS responsibly, others use them to take control of the claim and may charge for work that's overpriced, unnecessary, or even never completed. Once you've signed an AOB, you could be cut out of the conversation entirely. And in some cases, you may end up in the middle of a legal dispute between the contractor and your insurance company. Let's start with the pros. Convenience. An AOB means you won't have to deal directly with the insurance company. The contractor takes care of it for you. Faster repairs. Some contractors will get started right away, even while the claim is still being processed. Professional handling. And some experienced vendors really do know how to navigate insurance paperwork, which can be a headache. Now, here's where you need to be careful. The cons. Loss of control. Once you sign, the contractor can make decisions about the claim without checking in with you. Inflated charges. If they overcharge and your insurer refuses to pay the full bill, guess who's stuck with the difference? You. Legal issues. In some cases, AOS have led to lawsuits and the homeowner got pulled right into the middle of it. Quality concerns. And if the contractor gets paid upfront, some might cut corners or even disappear altogether.

Welcome to the (somewhat) inaugural episode of "Contractor Talk with Richie Kidwell," now exclusively on podcast! Dive deep into the evolving landscape of restoration contracting in Florida with Richie and our esteemed guest, Hans Kennon, a seasoned attorney known for his expertise and impeccable style. In this 30-minute episode, we unravel the complex shift from Assignment of Benefits (AOB) contracts to Direction to Pay agreements, exploring their impacts on contractors, homeowners, and the insurance industry. 

Discover the rich history of AOB in Florida, a state known for its susceptibility to natural disasters and the critical role of restoration contractors in the aftermath. Hans Kennon, with his decades of legal experience, brings valuable insights into the pros, cons, and future implications of this pivotal transition. Say goodbye to the constraints of short segments and two-hour marathons; our podcast format allows us to explore topics like these in greater depth than ever before.

Join us as we embark on this new journey, providing restoration contractors, industry professionals, and anyone interested in the intricacies of Florida's legal landscape with the knowledge they need to navigate these changes. Don't forget to subscribe for more insightful discussions on restoration contracting and beyond.

back in 2014, 2015, when I first, you know, got involved. And so that was one of the first

because it really is such a valuable tool for contractors to be able to use.

metadata.title: Do You Have to Pay Your Deductible If the Accident Wasn't Your Fault?
metadata.author: Collision Crash Course
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of Collision Crash Course, Meghan explains one of the most confusing parts of filing an auto insurance claim: paying your deductible when someone else caused the accident.

Imagine someone rear-ends you at a stoplight. Your vehicle needs $5,000 in repairs, but your insurance company tells you that you're responsible for a $1,000 deductible.

How is that fair when you didn't cause the accident?

In this video, we break down:

✅ What an auto insurance deductible actually is

✅ The difference between using your own insurance and the at-fault driver's insurance

✅ When you may not have to pay a deductible

✅ What subrogation means and how deductible reimbursement works

✅ Why getting your deductible refunded isn't always guaranteed

✅ Three questions every consumer should ask before filing a claim

THE BOTTOM LINE:

Being not at fault doesn't automatically eliminate your deductible. Understanding your coverage and which insurance company is handling the claim can make a big difference.

At Collision Crash Course, our mission is to make automotive, insurance, and collision repair information easy for everyday consumers to understand.

🚘 Know before you're in a collision!

💬 Have you ever paid a deductible for an accident you didn't cause? Tell us about your experience in the comments.

👍 Like, subscribe, and share to help other drivers become informed consumers.

Insurance coverage and deductible recovery vary by policy, state, fault determination, and claim circumstances. This video provides general consumer education.

#CollisionCrashCourse #AutoInsurance #InsuranceDeductible #NotAtFault #CarAccident #InsuranceClaims #CollisionRepair #CarInsuranceTips

metadata.title: A New Era of Estimating | Your Data, Your Expertise, From Scope to Estimate — Webinar
metadata.author: Encircle
metadata.shortDescription:
Do you want your estimates fast or defensible? You shouldn't have to choose. A new era of estimating has begun.

The old way: every tech documents a different way, an estimator builds a scope from notes and instinct, and the number gets picked apart on the adjuster’s desk.

We’ve spent fourteen years building it: structured, IICRC-aligned job data, captured the same reliable way on every job, even offline. That’s not a feature. That’s the thing that had to exist first.

The new era: now that data—the photos, videos, notes, moisture readings, floor plans you already capture—fuels a scope and estimate in Xactimate, with sketch, line items and all in just minutes. Your estimator applies their judgement and experience to review and refine rather than building it from scratch.

0:00:00 - Introduction
0:07:04 - Encircle AI in Restoration
0:11:39 - Encircle Scope to Estimate Demo
0:19:00 - Chat with David Herring
0:31:23 - What to do: The First 10 Minutes and Beyond
0:43:19 - Promo Video
0:45:08 - Live Q/A
0:55:42 - Conclusion

Download the app from:
Apple App Store: https://itunes.apple.com/us/app/encircle/id604527488
Google Play Store: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.encircle

Find out more at https://getencircle.com/

So, I don't want to leave contaminated items overnight in my pro my cleaning room or my processing center. I don't recommend just opening up all your packages in an open warehouse where you have all kinds of other things. It needs to be contained in your processing center again with proper air filtration and HEPA uh air scrubbing going on. You should also obviously be wearing proper PPE, right? So that you're not your uh team is not getting exposed to all of those contaminants. And then at the end of every single day, the reason I don't want these contaminated items staying in there overnight is because yes, your center should be properly cleaned and decontaminated so that that is is ready for the next day and you're not leaving contaminants in the area. Okay. So the third question that Sam had is this cleaning procedures at the warehouse. After unpacking, furniture would typically be typically be cleaned with HEPA vacuuming. Dishes and kitchen wear would be soaked and washed in a sink. Small items would be cleaning would be cleaned using a HEPA vacuum and dry sponge. Once all items have been cleaned, should they be placed into a chamber for fogging or is fogging necessary? Alternatively, should an ozone chamber be used before repacking and returning the items? Okay, so first off, after unpacking the furniture, it would typically be cleaned with a HEPA vacuum. I would absolutely hepo. Um the the furniture for sure, but that furniture may actually need to be steam cleaned. Okay, so HEPA vacuum may not be the only thing that you do. If it's a leather couch, then you're going to need to use a leather cleaner to be able to clean that couch to properly decontaminate it as well. And some of that furniture might even have wood on it that you may need to use like a woodcraft um and or you know some kind of a mild degrease or wet clean on that part of the furniture. Okay. So the next thing you said dishes and kitchen wear would be soaked and washed in a sink. So I prefer to wash my kitchen wear and dishes in an ultrasonic machine. It is going to do a much better and faster, more efficient, thus profitable cleaning of your items than just putting them in a sink and scrubbing them by hand. Now, when you do the ultrasonic processing system, you also are doing a pre-oak in that process. Okay? And then your next piece of this was small items would be cleaned using a HEPA vacuum and dry sponge. It depends on the small item. So, is this something that is what we call dippable? Can it get wet? Can I use it? Put it in the ultrasonic machine. That's what I would prefer to do if I can because it's a more thorough cleaning and it's faster. Okay. More efficient. If it's small items that you need to clean dry method, then absolutely a hea vacuuming and using a dry cleaning sponge is what I would recommend. Depending on the item like book or artwork, that's a dry cleaning method. You might even want to use a a art gum eraser, which is another awesome tool to have in your arsenal for cleaning and decontamination. Okay. And then you said, "Once all items have been cleaned, should they be placed in a chamber for fogging or is fogging necessary? I used a fog in the past. I don't fog anymore." Okay. So, I I don't do that at all. Alternatively, should an ozone chamber be used before repacking, returning the items? I would say absolutely not. I do not like ozone. Ozone is dangerous. Um, it's very problematic and it can actually cause secondary odors and damage to certain items. For instance, you cannot ozone an item if it is damp or wet. You will bleach it and cause uh breakdown of the item. Leather, when you ozone leather, you literally can take years off of the life of the leather. So, I don't like ozone. My preferable me um method for odor removal is hydroxil. Now, I have a specific hydroxil I like to use um because they're not all the same. And hydroxil is more of a natural process. It does not damage items. It doesn't harm you. Humans can walk around in it while it's running. It's not going to uh damage you if you have a properly set up in the proper square footage. Okay? And and it doesn't cause secondary odor. I find it removes the odor and gives it more like a fresh new smell instead of a chemical smell, which is what ozone winds up doing. Okay. Oh, and also you can hydroxil item even when it's wet, which is great. So, I set my hydroxil and I deodorize in my drying chamber. Okay. So, your fourth question was handling of mattresses. Given that mattresses were covered with sheeting and bedding, would they still be considered affected by soot and smoke? Should they be disposed of or is there an effective cleaning process that can restore them? Excellent question. So, I still process the mattresses even if they're completely the bed's completely made. If the bed is not made, that might be a different story. This is very important in your onboarding process with your homeowner or your client that you walk through this with them and find out how they're where they're at. The level of contamination obviously matters and how bad the fire was. And how do they feel? Are they like, "Listen, I don't care what you do to this mattress. I'm not putting my head on it. I'm not laying on this." People get very sensitive when it comes to their bedding pillows and a mattress. Okay. Almost as a general rule, I log nonrestorable the bed pillows. So, ways to handle a mattress, obviously removing all the bedding, you know, was it made? Was it not made? That matters. Hepa vacuuming it, and then doing a steam cleaning on that mattress. metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of The Octagon Cleaning & Restoration Podcast, we sit down with Brindi Riley, a seasoned project manager with over 11 years at Octagon Cleaning and Restoration. Brindi shares her journey from cleaning technician to leadership, highlighting her passion for fire damage restoration. She takes us through the intricate process of fire mitigation—from environmental controls to odor removal—while emphasizing the emotional and logistical challenges of helping families recover. Tune in for an inside look at the restoration industry, the importance of clear client communication, and the dedication it takes to bring homes back to life.

#FireDamageRestoration #RestorationExperts #FireMitigation

Learn more: https://octagonrestoration.com/services/fire-smoke-damage/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video_description&utm_campaign=podcast

Stop wasting budget on Google Ads by tracking your actual lead conversion rates. This breakdown shows you how to stop paying for clicks that never turn into jobs.

Many water damage restoration business owners see traffic coming in but fail to realize that only a fraction of those clicks lead to paid work. This video explains how to audit your Google Ads performance by analyzing search terms and campaign settings to ensure you are only paying for high-intent visitors. For restoration business owners doing 500K to 5M a year, understanding the specific impact of your account changes is the only way to stop the bleed.

We look at how to implement a consistent Monday 20 minute routine to review your search terms and adjust your negative keywords system. By making single, isolated changes, you can clearly see what drives results and what drains your wallet. Use this process to refine your emergency lead generation and ensure your marketing spend is actually hitting your bottom line.

metadata.title: How do you set up Google Ads for emergency contractors in 2026?
metadata.author: PushLeads
metadata.shortDescription:
This video walks through how to set up high-intent Google Ads campaigns for emergency restoration contractors in 2026, covering keyword structure, negative keywords, call-first design, landing pages, call tracking, and the LSA migration into Performance Max. It is for water damage, fire damage, and storm damage contractors who have tried Google Ads before and burned budget on the wrong clicks.

When cost per click runs $50 to $100, every unqualified click hurts. The difference between a campaign that works and one that drains your budget usually comes down to search intent, not ad spend. This guide gives you the exact structure to filter out DIY searchers and job seekers and pay only for the homeowner standing in two inches of water who needs you right now.

- Use urgency modifiers like "emergency," "24/7," "near me," and "same day" to build a high-intent keyword list, and run exact match or tight phrase match only — never broad match
- Preload negative keywords before launch covering job seekers, DIY researchers, price shoppers, and cities outside your dispatch area, then review your search terms report weekly
- Design every campaign around phone calls, not form fills — run call assets in every ad, drive the phone number, and make sure someone answers live at 2 a.m.
- Raise bids on nights and weekends when competitors go dark, and set geo targeting to a tight radius around your real dispatch area, not the whole metro
- Build a focused landing page with a large click-to-call button above the fold, a response promise, trust badges, and reviews visible without scrolling
- Set conversions to calls longer than one minute using CallRail or similar call tracking, feed that data back to Google for smart bidding, and audit your LSA migration into the new Performance Max account because Google is not completing those migrations correctly

Chapters:
0:00 High-Intent Google Ads for Emergency Contractors
0:37 Search Intent Problem Costing You Money
1:29 DIY Searchers vs Emergency Buyers
2:57 High-Intent Keyword Blueprint
3:57 Negative Keywords as Budget Armor
4:56 Call-First Campaign Design
5:30 Time-Based Bidding and Geo Targeting
6:17 60-Second Landing Page Structure
7:07 Call Tracking and Conversion Setup
7:51 LSA Migration into Google Ads PMax
9:34 15-Minute Weekly Ops Checklist

Most emergency contractors don't have a Google Ads problem - they have a search intent problem. In this video I walk through the exact high-intent campaign setup we use for restoration, plumbing, roofing and 24/7 home-service companies: urgency keywords, negative keyword armor, call-first campaigns, ad-schedule bid boosts, and qualified-call tracking - plus the 2026 LSA to Performance Max migration that silently reset bids about 40% below Google's suggested ranges in one of our client accounts.

Google is killing the standalone Local Service Ads dashboard. metadata.title: Why Contractors Lose Margin After the Job Is Sold
metadata.author: George Gabriel
metadata.shortDescription:
Join our Skool community: https://www.skool.com/claude-for-roofers-7116

If you own a roofing company, or really any contracting business, you've had a job that looked good the day it sold and came in thinner by the time it was done. Part of that is markup math: put 50% on a $10,000 job and you keep 33%, not 50%. But a lot of what you lose goes after the job is sold, because nobody writes down what the job should cost before it starts, so a job that slides only shows up at the end of the year.

The example is a roofing job, but the job budget works the same for any contractor.

What's in the video:
• Markup vs margin in one minute, and how to price for the margin you actually want
• What your gross profit still has to pay before any of it is yours
• How a second dump haul, a supply run and a surprise second layer turn 33% into 25%
• The job budget at signing: by phase, adding back to the contract price to the dollar
• Why it matters even more on insurance jobs, where the scope sets most of the price and your cost is what you control
• An AI tool that builds the budget for you, flags anything not priced, and never changes your price

What you can do tonight:
1. Pull up your last finished job and write down what it sold for.
2. Write down what it really cost, line by line: materials, crew, dump, permit, anything else.
3. Price minus cost, divided by price. That's your real margin. Compare it to what you thought you'd make.

I'm not a roofer. I help roofing companies doing over $1 million a year save more time and make more money using AI. Everything on screen is a practice company, so the names and numbers are made up. Net profit range from JobNimbus (a roofing software company). This isn't accounting advice; check your numbers with your bookkeeper.

Want the job budget set up on your own jobs? I show you how inside the community:
https://www.skool.com/claude-for-roofers-7116

#roofing #contractors #roofingbusiness

In this video, I will go step by step into how to use a scope sheet. I will explain why I think you should be using a scope sheet. I will give you a digital copy of my scope sheets just for liking this video and asking me for the scope sheets in the comments. 

This free tutorial you will see how to develop your own scope sheet to fit your needs. 

This video is part of our Step by Step Claims Process found in this playlist:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLr8YoVmw127eG7Pv5FbUXpbLWzY_7vONr

If you subscribe to my channel and leave me a message in the comments to let me know, I will send you an updated contact list of over 70 IA firms across the US. You can use this list to contact as many of them as you choose and get on their deployment lists.   

Check out https://adjusterpedia.com/ to learn more about insurance adjusting, free xactimate tutorials, adjusting tools and much more. If you are a new adjuster trying to break into the adjusting business, adjusterpedia.com can help you land your first deployment and help you get consistent work as an independent adjuster. 

Contact me at adjusterpedia@gmail.com if you would like to request a video on a specific topic related to adjusting or Xactimate or you would like a digital copy of my scope sheets to do with as you please.
