metadata.title: Understanding Water Mitigation: From the Loss to the Estimate | ReconSmart
metadata.author: ReconSmart Solutions LLC
metadata.shortDescription:
Water mitigation is more than removing water and setting drying equipment.

In this ReconSmart training video, we break down how a water loss moves from the initial assessment through extraction, structural drying, moisture monitoring, documentation, and ultimately the restoration estimate.

We also explain important restoration concepts including water Category vs. Class, air movers, dehumidification, air filtration, moisture readings, drying goals, field documentation, MICA, and how documented mitigation work is translated into Xactimate.

The central principle is simple:

A strong mitigation estimate tells the same story as the field documentation.

This video references principles associated with the ANSI/IICRC S500 Standard for Professional Water Damage Restoration. It is educational content and is not affiliated with or endorsed by IICRC.

Learn more about ReconSmart Solutions and our restoration industry resources at reconsmartsolutions.com.

#WaterMitigation #Restoration #Xactimate #RestorationEstimating #WaterDamage #StructuralDrying #IICRCS500 #PropertyClaims #ReconSmart

segments.text: Hey everyone, and welcome to this
explainer. Today, we're going on a
practical ride-along to completely
demystify professional water mitigation.
We are going to bridge that tricky gap
between what actually happens out in the
field and the final financial estimate,
all based on the foundational principles
of the ANSI/IICRC
S500 standard. Whether you're brand new
to restoration estimating or you're just
looking to sharpen up your existing
skills, I am absolutely thrilled to
guide you through this. So, let's dive
right in.
Okay, picture this. You're an estimator
and you're approaching a brand new job.
Is this the very first thing you should
be thinking about? I mean, is your
immediate instinct to open up your
software and just start hunting for
billing codes to build out a scope?
Well, the answer is a resounding no. And
this brilliantly illustrates our core
philosophy for today. Your software,
like Xactimate, doesn't determine the
scope of a mitigation job. The physical
loss determines the scope. We have to
start by asking, "What actually happened
at this property? What was physically
affected?" The documented loss and the
necessary work that was actually
performed, that's what drives the
estimate, not some desire to hit a
specific dollar amount. Ultimately, the
estimate is just the financial
representation of a physical reality.
To get us to that final estimate, here
is our road map. We're going to cover
evaluating the water loss, category
versus class, extraction and demolition,
the science of drying, documenting the
job, and finally, the final estimate.
Section one, evaluating the water loss,
the scene of the crime. You know,
mitigation isn't just about mindlessly
throwing a bunch of drying equipment
into a building. It requires a really
strategic initial assessment before the
drying can even begin.
A restoration pro has to understand the
unique conditions of that specific loss.
Where did the water come from? And
crucially, what's the extent of its
migration?
Because water is incredibly sneaky. It
can migrate invisibly well beyond the
immediate area, traveling through
subflooring, wicking up wall cavities,
soaking into insulation, and just hiding
out in the framing.
You also have to assess environmental
conditions and safety hazards like
electrical dangers or slip risks before
a single piece of equipment is even
placed. Section two, category versus
class.
Knowing the difference. So, these are
literally two of the most frequently
confused terms in the entire restoration
industry. Category is strictly about
toxicity and contamination. Is the water
sanitary like a clean pipe burst? Well,
that's category one. Or is it grossly
contaminated with harmful agents like a
sewage backup? That'd be category three.
Class, on the other hand, has absolutely
nothing to do with contamination. Class
is all about the evaporation load. It
measures how much material is wet, how
deeply that water was absorbed, and how
hard it's going to be to dry it out. So,
the big takeaway here is this. A
category three water loss is not

The restoration industry is known for its recession-proof nature, and Alex shares how, with proper business management, it can be highly lucrative.

metadata.title: Public Adjusters: Stop Wasting Hours Building Xactimate Estimates
metadata.author: American Roof Supplements
metadata.shortDescription:
👉 Your first Xactimate estimate or supplement is FREE. Book a 10-minute setup call with Joe: https://bit.ly/ARS-FreeSupplement
No monthly fees, no minimums. Pay per job: $50 per estimate, $150 per supplement.

If you're a licensed public adjuster spending hours building Xactimate estimates yourself, the real problem may not be Xactimate.

It may be your workflow.

Public adjusters already have to inspect losses, communicate with insureds, review carrier documents, organize evidence, manage claim files, and handle the licensed work that only they are authorized to perform.

Then somebody still has to build the estimate.

In this video, we break down why estimate production can become a major bottleneck for public-adjusting firms, how back-end Xactimate estimating support can fit into the workflow, and why outsourcing technical estimate production does not mean giving up control of the claim.

We cover:

• Where public adjusters lose time in the estimating process  
• Why building every estimate yourself can limit capacity  
• How measurements, photos, notes, carrier estimates, and supporting documents fit into an efficient handoff  
• Why the licensed public adjuster should still review the final estimate  
• How back-end estimating support can help during high-volume storm periods  
• The difference between technical estimating support and licensed public adjusting  
• Why documentation quality still matters even when the estimate is outsourced

American Roof Supplements prepares residential Xactimate estimates, supplements, and supporting construction documentation for roofing contractors, licensed public adjusters, and other property professionals.

We organize legitimate construction scope using measurements, photos, product information, notes, and supported construction or code-related operations.

American Roof Supplements is not a public-adjusting company or law firm. We do not determine coverage, interpret insurance policies, negotiate claims, or guarantee approval. Those responsibilities remain with the appropriate licensed professionals and the carrier.

👉 https://www.estimatehub.com/articles/xactimate-estimate-example

In this video, we walk through a real Xactimate estimate example and explain how Xactimate estimates are structured. If you're new to Xactimate or trying to understand how insurance estimates are built, this walkthrough will help you see how line items, quantities, and scope information come together inside an estimate.

Xactimate is one of the most widely used estimating platforms in the property insurance and restoration industries. Contractors, adjusters, and estimators use it to calculate repair costs for property damage such as water, fire, and storm claims.

Chapters
0:00 Introduction
0:15 Xactimate Review - Claim Info
1:35 Xactimate Sketch 
1:55 Xactimate Estimate Items
3:05 Xactimate Photos 
3:15 Print Xactimate estimate
3:30 Xactimate estimate review
4:10 Contractor and Adjuster reconciliation review
5:15 Final Thoughts

In this tutorial you’ll learn:
• What a Xactimate estimate looks like
• How line items are organized inside an estimate
• How rooms and folders structure the scope of work
• How contractors and adjusters review estimates

Understanding how estimates are built in Xactimate is essential for anyone working with property damage claims.

👉 https://www.estimatehub.com

Filing a hail damage insurance claim after a hail or windstorm? What you do in the first few days decides whether your insurer pays for a new roof or you fight a denial for months.
This step-by-step guide covers storm damage from the first 24 hours to the final check, including what to do if the payout falls short.

FREE Wind & Hail Claim Checklist (follows this video step by step): https://homeownerexplained.com/wind-hail-claim-checklist/

Learned you have a big percentage deductible or actual-cash-value roof coverage? Compare homeowners insurance quotes: https://homeownerexplained.com/go/compare-rates/

In this video:
- Why it's your claim (and why not to jump on the neighborhood "claim train")
- The first 24 hours: safety, temporary repairs, receipts, additional living expenses
- How to document hail and wind damage from the ground like an adjuster
- Your wind/hail deductible, replacement cost vs actual cash value, and claim deadlines
- Filing, the adjuster visit, and reading the estimate line by line
- 4 storm chaser red flags
- Recoverable depreciation, mortgage checks, supplements, and what to do if you're denied or underpaid

0:00 What to do after a hail or windstorm

8:16 Getting paid, and what to do if it's not enough
9:33 Recap and outro

metadata.author: Tradeforge CRM
metadata.shortDescription:
The full roofing + storm restoration + insurance workflow inside TradeForge. Storm rolls through. You pull every hail and wind event onto your dashboard, attach it to the customer, snap damage photos, order the EagleView, upload the carrier's lowball Xactimate, and the AI writes the supplement letter with the codes, the math, and the manufacturer specs cited. Then the contract goes out for e-sign. You can run this whole thing from your truck.

Built for roofers, restoration, exteriors, mitigation, siding, and anyone who deals with insurance as part of the job.

In this walkthrough you'll see how a roofer in TradeForge:
✅ Pulls every NOAA hail and wind event in the area, attaches it to the claim (adjusters will ask for it)
✅ Opens an insurance claim with carrier, policy number, claim number — all attached to the contact
✅ Uploads damage photos — AI tags every damage point with the code citation
✅ Orders an EagleView roof measurement straight from the lead — auto-attaches when the report drops
✅ Uploads the carrier's Xactimate PDF — AI writes the supplement letter with your state's code cited
✅ Sends the contract for e-signature with state-specific clauses generated for you
✅ All in one CRM where you only pay for the shit you actually use — insurance pack is its own SKU, GCs don't pay for it

⏱️ TIMESTAMPS
0:00 — Intro (built for roofers, mitigation, siding, all insurance trades)
0:15 — Pull NOAA storm data + tag the hail/wind event to the client
1:00 — Open the insurance claim in the system
1:34 — AI damage photo analysis with code citations
2:36 — Order an EagleView roof measurement from the lead
3:06 — Upload the carrier's Xactimate → AI writes the supplement letter (Ohio code cited)
4:02 — Create the contract, link the estimate, send for e-signature
5:41 — Why insurance is its own pack (you only pay for what you actually use)
6:22 — Recap + 14-day trial, no card

🔗 LINKS
Start your 14-day free trial → https://tradeforgeworks.com?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=roofer-demo
See all features → https://tradeforgeworks.com/for/roofers
Book an Enterprise discovery call → https://tradeforgeworks.com/enterprise/contact

WHO THIS IS FOR
Roofers, storm restoration companies, exterior contractors, mitigation crews, siding installers, and anyone who deals with insurance claims as part of the job. If you've ever eaten a supplement because you couldn't prove the code citation in time, this is for you.

WHY TRADEFORGE
Built by a contractor. AI-native, not retrofitted. The supplement engine is purpose-built for storm and restoration trades — most general CRMs (Jobber, HousecallPro, ServiceTitan) don't have it. EagleView and NOAA storm data ride in the box.

#TradeForge #RoofingCRM #InsuranceSupplement #StormRestoration

metadata.title: Xactimate 101 How Roofing Supplements Actually Work (Beginner’s Guide)
metadata.author: American Roof Supplements
metadata.shortDescription:
👉 Your first Xactimate estimate or supplement is FREE. Book a 10-minute setup call with Joe: https://bit.ly/ARS-FreeSupplement
No monthly fees, no minimums. Pay per job: $50 per estimate, $150 per supplement.

New to Xactimate and roofing supplements? This beginner-friendly guide breaks down how the process actually works—from reading the carrier’s estimate to identifying legitimate missing items, documenting the differences, and preparing a professional supplement.

A roofing supplement is not simply a request for more money. It is a documented request to correct or add legitimate work that may be missing, measured incorrectly, underestimated, or otherwise not reflected in the carrier’s current scope.

In this video, you’ll learn:

• What Xactimate actually is
• How to read a carrier’s roof estimate
• What a roofing supplement really does
• How the supplement process works step by step
• What documentation helps support a supplement
• How measurements, photos, bids, invoices, and code references may be used
• What a supplement can—and cannot—change
• Five common beginner mistakes
• How to build a repeatable supplement workflow
• Why roofing contractors outsource Xactimate estimating and supplement writing

Remember:

Xactimate is the estimating tool.
The supplement is the documented correction.

A supplement can help document legitimate missing or incorrect scope, but it cannot rewrite the insurance policy, remove the homeowner’s deductible, create coverage for excluded damage, turn ACV into RCV, or guarantee approval.

Need help with your Xactimate estimates or roofing supplements?

American Roof Supplements prepares professional residential Xactimate estimates and supplements for roofing contractors.

✓ First estimate or supplement FREE for new customers
✓ No monthly fee
✓ No minimum number of jobs
✓ Free revisions
✓ Professional company-branded documents

Pricing:

Residential Xactimate Estimate — $50
Follow-Up Supplement — $100 when we prepared the original estimate
Standalone Residential Supplement — $150

Schedule an appointment:
AmericanRoofSupplements.com

Subscribe for more videos about roofing insurance claims, Xactimate estimating, supplements, carrier estimates, adjuster meetings, and roofing-business operations.

Disclaimer: This video is for general educational purposes only and is not legal, insurance, or financial advice. Coverage and claim decisions depend on the specific policy, supporting documentation, applicable requirements, and carrier review.

segments.text: If you're new to insurance restoration,
an exactimate estimate can look like a
wall of codes, quantities, unit prices,
depreciation, and line items that only
an adjuster could love. Then somebody
tells you, we need to supplement this
claim. And now the question becomes,
supplement what exactly? Here's the
simple answer. Exactate is a tool used
to build detailed property repair
estimates. A roofing supplement is not a
second claim, and it is not a magic way
to make an insurance company pay more.
It is a documented request to correct or
add legitimate work that is missing,
measured incorrectly, priced
differently, based on supportable
information, or otherwise not reflected
in the carrier's current scope. In this
beginner's guide, we're going to break
down what exactate actually does, how to
read a roofing estimate, how supplements
are built, what documentation matters,
what a supplement can and cannot change,
and the beginner mistakes that create
unnecessary delays. Exactimate is
property claims estimating software from
Verisque. Contractors, restoration
professionals, and claims adjusters use
it to create detailed repair estimates
using sketches, line items, quantities,
pricing, notes, photographs, and
reports. Instead of writing one broad
line that says, "Replace the roof." An
exactimate estimate breaks the project
into individual operations. You may see
separate items for removing shingles,
installing shingles, underllayment,
starter, ridge cap, flashing, vents,
pipe boots, disposal, steep slope work,
and other operations that apply to that
specific project. Each line item has a
description and quantity, and exactoate
line items can include material, labor,
and equipment components. Before adding
another item, understand what the
existing item already includes.
Exactimate also uses price lists that
can be selected by geographic area
including city or zip code. Labor and
material costs are not identical from
one market to another. So the selected
price list matters. But remember
something important. Exactimate is an
estimating platform. It does not decide
insurance coverage. A line item existing
in Exactoate does not automatically mean
the homeowner's policy covers it. And
adding an item to an estimate does not
guarantee the carrier will approve it.
Before you can write a good supplement,
you need to understand the estimate you
already have. Do not look only at the
grand total. Start with the scope. What
roof area did the carrier measure? What
quantities did they use? What materials
and operations are included? What was
removed? What is being replaced? What
accessories are listed? What labor
operations are included? What price list
was used? Are there notes attached to
important line items? And does the
estimate include a sketch that matches
the actual structure? Exactimate reports
can include line item details,
summaries, and sketches. The total is
only the result. The scope tells you how
they got there. Your real question is,
does this estimate accurately describe
the legitimate work required at this
property? A supplement begins when there
is a legitimate difference between the
current estimate and the supported scope
of work. Maybe the roof measurement is
wrong. Maybe the carrier estimate
includes 30 squares but the measurement
report supports 32. Maybe a damaged pipe
boot is visible in the photographs but
is not listed. Maybe starter, ridge cap,
flashing, ventilation, or another
necessary component is absent. Maybe
specialty work requires a bid. Maybe an
applicable building code requirement
creates additional necessary work
subject to the policy and local
requirements. Maybe the available
documentation supports a different
material or labor cost. The supplement
takes those differences and presents
them in an organized way. Insurers
themselves recognize supplements as a
way to provide estimates or information
supporting additional repair costs that
were not included in the original

Marketing Ninjas helps restoration companies build an army of loyal referral partners—without spending a dime on PPC or SEO.
We make it easy to scale with real relationships, not risky ads.

Thanks for watching—and God bless!

metadata.title: One Question That Will Shake the Billion-Dollar Insurance Restoration Industry
metadata.author: Grossman PA LLC
metadata.shortDescription:
We're challenging an entire billion-dollar industry with ONE question. And I doubt the people being challenged will have the courage to answer it.

Mitigation contractors. Restoration companies. Insurance adjusters. Public adjusters. It's time for accountability.

For decades, homeowners have been caught between contractors and insurance companies, hearing accusations of lowballing, inflated estimates, delayed payments, and promises to fight for every dollar.

But what if the real problem isn't who you think it is?

We're asking a question this industry needs to confront.

We're inviting contractors to respond publicly, explain their position, and defend their practices.

Next week, ClaimHelpMe delivers its answer.

No fighting. No empty promises. Just construction knowledge, documented facts, and accountability.

SCOPE IT. DOCUMENT IT. SUPPORT IT.

metadata.title: How he Overturned a Denied Insurance Claim | Public Adjuster Case Study & Expert Tips
metadata.author: The Adjuster's Roundtable
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of The Adjusters Round Table, we sit down with Daniel Kern, a licensed public insurance adjuster with Rockwall National Public Adjusters, who has successfully recovered over $11 million in claims for policyholders. He is licensed across Florida, Texas, North Carolina, and Georgia.

In this video, you'll learn:

How we overturned a denied hurricane damage insurance claim for full policy limits

Real-life insurance claim case study involving multiple property structures

The role of duties after loss and how they impact your claim outcome

Why documentation and expert support are critical in denied or underpaid claims

What policyholders need to know about proof of loss deadlines

How to avoid going straight to litigation and still get paid

Whether you're a homeowner, commercial property owner, real estate investor, property manager, or part of an HOA, this video provides valuable insight into how public adjusters help maximize insurance claims and fight for policyholder rights.

Rockwall National Public Adjusters works nationwide to help clients recover after hurricanes, storms, water damage, and more — without the stress of fighting the insurance company alone.

👉 Need help with a denied or underpaid insurance claim?
Visit us at: https://rockwallnpa.com
📧 Email: info@rockwallnpa.com
📞 Call us for a free policy review or storm damage consultation. 866-483-4001

🔔 Don’t forget to Like, Subscribe, and Share this video to help others navigate the insurance claim process.

Rockwall National Public Adjusters is licensed in multiple states, including Florida, Texas, and South Carolina. The information shared in this video is for general educational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. We are not attorneys, and viewers should consult a qualified attorney or licensed professional for advice on specific claims or legal matters.

metadata.title: Restoration Contractors: Stop Selling From Weakness! Insurance Claims Done Right
metadata.author: claimhelpme
metadata.shortDescription:
HOW TO DO INSURANCE RESTORATION RIGHT — REAL-WORLD EDUCATION.

Contractors, restoration companies, public adjusters, and homeowners: understanding the insurance restoration process BEFORE construction begins can prevent costly mistakes, unnecessary delays, and financial disputes.

Too many contractors tell homeowners, "We'll take the undisputed amount, start construction, supplement the difference, and go to appraisal if necessary."

That's not a strategy. That's selling from weakness instead of knowledge.

What happens when a contractor writes a $100,000 repair estimate and the insurance company allows only $34,000?

Do you start construction and hope the remaining $66,000 gets approved?

Or do you understand how to properly document, justify, and defend the legitimate construction scope before that inadequate payment becomes the working baseline?

This educational video explains how to approach the homeowner's first meeting, establish professional credibility, preserve evidence, and prepare for disagreements before they happen.

QUESTIONS THIS VIDEO ADDRESSES:
1. How should restoration contractors approach the first homeowner meeting?
2. What should contractors explain before asking homeowners to sign a contract?
3. What is an undisputed insurance claim payment?
4. Should contractors accept an inadequate undisputed amount?
5. Why should insurance estimates be reviewed immediately?
6. What happens when the carrier's estimate is substantially lower?
7. Can starting reconstruction destroy important claim evidence?
8. Why should contractors document damage before demolition?
9. Can contractors supplement an insurance estimate after construction begins?
10. What are the risks of relying on insurance appraisal?
11. How much can an insurance appraisal cost?
12. Why can missing documentation increase appraisal expenses?
13. What construction information can contractors explain without acting as public adjusters?
14. How can homeowners recognize knowledgeable restoration contractors?
15. How do proper estimating and documentation help prevent claim delays?

The objective isn't to promise additional insurance money. It's to establish the legitimate repair requirements, explain the process, and protect homeowners from unnecessary financial risk.

The next lesson explains why an inadequate undisputed amount can become one of the most expensive mistakes in an insurance claim.

SCOPE IT. DOCUMENT IT. SUPPORT IT.

Follow. Subscribe. Share.

metadata.title: Medicare Assignment of Benefit (AoB) in Gentu
metadata.author: Magentus | Practice Management
metadata.shortDescription:
In support of the Assignment of Benefit changes taking effect from 1 July 2026 - this video provides a walkthrough of Medicare AoB requirements.

What is changing in Gentu from 1 July 2026: 
☑️ A pre-assignment and post-assignment form will be available and there will no longer be a standard DB4 form. 
☑️ You will have the ability to track outstanding AOBs when you go to submit bulk-bill claims 
☑️ For both Bulk Bill and Simplified Billing through ECLIPSE, Gentu will prompt your declaration every time you raise a claim
☑️The Bulk Bill invoice screen will show an additional checkbox to confirm a valid AOB has been captured 
☑️ AOB is implied or requested radio buttons for Health Fund Claims

segments.text: Hello, my name is Timothy ankle. I'm a
partner here at Blackwater Mueller Cats
Craig. As most of you know, Hurricane
Matthew struck the US last week with
devastating results. Our office has been
fielding calls from insurance companies
with regard to Matthew, but also with
regard to an issue that's popped up here
in Florida over the last four years,
that is the assignment of benefits
issue. The purpose of this presentation
is to walk through the assignment of
benefit issue with you, to bring you up
to speed on how the assignment of
benefit issue may impact insurance
claims here in Florida, and talk about a
few legal issues that pop up with
assignment of benefit claims. For
shortand, I'm going to refer to these
sorts of claims as
AOPS. The first question a lot of people
have is what is an AOP? What is an
assignment of benefits?
Florida law has recognized the ability
of an insured to assign his or her
benefits after a loss to another for
approximately 100 years. In Florida, the
typical way an assignment of benefits
pops up in the insurance context is an
insurance company will issue a policy to
homeowner or a commercial business. And
after a loss, that homeowner or
commercial business owner will hire
contractors to either minimize the
damage or repair the
damage. When the contractor comes in to
ensure that he or she gets paid, the
contractor will have either the
homeowner or the commercial business
owner execute the assignment of
benefits. The insured typically will say
the scope of the damage that they'd like
repaired. The contractor will agree to
pay it. And when the insured executes
the AOB, that gives the contractor the
confidence that they will get paid
because they can make the claim directly
to the insurance company. Now, there are
a number of front-end issues uh that pop
up with
AOBS. For most folks who have dealt with
either a homeowners or commercial
insurance policy, you're aware that
there's often a provision in the policy
called an assignment provision or an
anti-assignment provision. So the first
question that we typically get from
folks is are AOBS legal? Are AOBS valid?
My insurance policy has an
anti-assignment
provision. The anti-assignment provision
in most insurance policies is there to
protect the insurance company in the
manner that they underwrote the
insurance policy. What those policy
provisions typically say is that you,
the insured, are not allowed to assign
the insurance policy to another without
the written consent of the insurer. The
purpose of this is to protect the
underwriting integrity of the insurer.
Here's an example. An insurer will
accept an application from an insured,
place a policy on the risk, and be
confident that they've underwrote it and
priced it properly. What that provision
in the insurance policy is intended to
do is prevent the insurer from
transferring that policy to a risk that
wasn't
underwritten. Florida law is clear that
that assignment anti-assignment
provision does not apply to post-loss
assignment of insurance benefits. So
most policies that have an
anti-assignment provision that just
prevents the policy from being
transferred to a different risk, but it
doesn't prohibit the assignment of
post-loss insurance benefits. So let's
take a common example. A homeowner has a
pipe break in her house. She calls out a
plumber or she calls out a water
extraction company. That company comes
to their house and will take an
assignment of benefits to do the work.
That contractor then will approach the
insurance company and make a claim
directly to the insurance company as
though that contractor is standing in
the shoes of the insured for purposes of
payment. There's a number of uses of
assignments in Florida law. They're not
just gerine to first party property law.
In the car accident world, we have
personal injury protection and
assignment of benefits have been used
there for decades with regard to medical
treatment. More recently, we've seen the
assignment of benefits being used in the

Specifically, whether or not the insurance company can assert the policy exclusions when dealing with an assigned claim. And the answer to that is yes. When a when a contractor takes an assignment of the claim, the contractor takes it subject to all the defenses that would have been available to the insured had the insured retain the claim. As such, when the insurance company handles the claim, they have the full complement of defenses under the policy that they would if the insured had the claim. That includes all the policies exclusions. In Florida, the burden is on the insurer to prove the applicability of any exclusion, including in an assigned claim. The asenee who's making the claim has the burden to prove that the uh claim is covered. A number of areas where we have seen uh asenee claims and particular exclusions apply is when there have been leakage or seepage claims. Most policies will include an exclusion for long-term seage and leakage. And these are often pipe break cases that require water extraction contractors. Those claims are probably more difficult to handle than others because they require an assessment of the time that the leak occurred and the duration of the leak persisting. those uh assigned claims can be even more difficult because many times the contractor has already performed all the work before the first notice of loss. Again, it's important to look at the assignment language and then handle the claim as you would as though the insured was providing it herself. In the big picture, those are the main issues that pop up when we see assignment of benefit claims. As we said, Hurricane Matthew has created an avalanche of claims here in Florida, and we anticipate many of these will be assigned claims. If you have any questions regarding assignments, how to interpret them, their validity, or questions during the claim process, please reach out and call us. We'd love to help you.

A $900 fender bender with a $500 deductible can cost you $2,300 if you file the claim. Here's the math nobody runs before calling their insurer — plus the three exceptions, and the homeowner surprise with percentage deductibles.

0:49 What a deductible actually is
1:15 Per claim, not per year

5:32 Comprehensive claims
6:02 Never pay cash for someone's bumper

metadata.shortDescription:
Is it possible to legally "COVER" the insurance deductible? Actually, yes, it is! But it absolute depends on how it is done. There are many methods not so advisable that a great deal of roofing contractors and restoration contractors use to "waive" the insurance deductible.

This is absolutely reckless and not necessary at all. Especially since there are many LEGAL methods that can be deployed, which will keep the contractor out of trouble, as well as minimize liability to the property owner, which should be most important after all.

In This Video:
Discover the ins and outs of insurance deductibles in this comprehensive guide. We cover what a deductible is, when it's applied, and how to explain it to policyholders effectively. Whether you're an adjuster, a homeowner, or just interested in understanding more about insurance, this video will provide you with the knowledge you need.

Key Topics Covered:

Introduction to Deductibles - Learn what a deductible is and its role in insurance policies.

The Purpose of Deductibles - Explore the reasoning behind deductibles and how they can affect your premiums.

Applying the Deductible - Understand when and how deductibles are applied during the claims process.

Explaining Deductibles to Policyholders - Tips and strategies for explaining deductibles to homeowners in a clear and understandable way.

Real-Life Examples - Real-world scenarios to illustrate the impact of deductibles on insurance claims.

segments.text: Master the claim rules that separate a
correct adjuster answer from a costly
exam trap, who gets salvage, when
subrogation applies, and how fair claims
duties work.
One shortcut later will help you
distinguish a coverage issue from an
unfair claims practices violation. This
video is part of our free insurance
adjuster license exam prep series. The
playlist and notes PDF links are in the
description, so please follow the
playlist in order.
Let's begin. This lesson builds the
claim handling chain from the damaged
property itself to recovery from
responsible third parties.
You will distinguish salvage from
subrogation because one concerns
remaining property and the other
concerns a payment claim against someone
else. We will also separate fraud
indicators from actual proof of
intentional wrongdoing.
Ethical duties include honesty,
competence, confidentiality,
impartiality, and staying within
authority. Finally, we will connect fair
claims practices with catastrophe work
where urgency never excuses poor
investigation or unsupported
conclusions. This is video four of four
in the insurance adjuster license exam
prep playlist. Watch them in order and
you will find all the links in the
description.
This chapter begins with the rights that
arise after a covered loss.
First, we will examine salvage, meaning
property that remains after damage.
Next, we will compare it with
subrogation, which reaches outward
toward a responsible third party. We
will then introduce fraud and the
ethical standards that keep claim
decisions fair.
Keep one central idea in mind. Payment
does not remove the adjuster's duty to
investigate, document, and act honestly.
Think of salvage as what is left after a
covered loss, not as a separate kind of
insurance coverage.
It may be a damaged vehicle, building
materials, equipment, or personal
property that still has value.
That value come from use, resale, parts,
or recycling. After payment, the insurer
may take possession or control of the
property, but the exact result depends
on the policy, the settlement, and
applicable law.
In some claims, the owner keeps the
damaged property and the settlement
reflects that choice. The adjuster must
protect the property from additional
damage and document its condition.
The property should then be inspected
and its value estimated before it is
sold, transferred, or discarded. For
example, a damaged vehicle may become
insurer controlled salvage after the
claim is settled and the insurer takes
possession.
The key exam point is that salvage
concerns remaining damaged property. Do
not confuse that property or its value
with a recovery action against a
negligent third party.
Salvage handling starts by protecting
the remaining property from theft,
weather, or further damage.
The adjuster then inspects and records
its condition with photographs,
measurements, and relevant statements.
Next, the value of the salvage is
estimated using appropriate evidence
rather than an unsupported guess.
The claim is settled according to the
policy, valuation method, deductible,
limits, and the agreed treatment of the
property. Finally, every transfer, sale,
storage decision, or disposal should be
documented.
This sequence protects both the claim
file and the parties' rights.
Salvage and subrogation are both
recovery concepts, but they point in
different directions.
Salvage concerns the damaged property
that remains after the covered loss and
may produce value through reuse, sale,
or parts. Subrogation concerns the
insurer's right to seek repayment from a
responsible third party after paying the
insured loss.
Salvage requires attention to
possession, condition, valuation,
storage, and disposal. Subrogation
requires attention to fault, payment,
legal rights, notices, protection
against releases.
The exam trap is to treat either one as
a second payment to the claimant. The no
double recovery principle prevents that
result.
Subrogation is the insurer's right to
pursue someone else who caused a loss
after the insurer has paid the claim.
In simple terms, the insurer steps into
the policy holder's legal shoes for that
recovery. The rule exists because the
responsible third party should
ultimately bear the cost rather than the
insurer or the policy holder.
Payment of the covered claim is usually
the key event that activates the
insurer's recovery rights. The insurer
can then investigate fault, notify the
responsible parties, and seek
reimbursement.
The policy holder is not supposed to
receive payment from both the insurer
and the person who caused the same
damage. That is the double recovery
principle. The policy holder also should
not sign a release that destroys the
insurer's recovery rights without proper
coordination.
For example, after paying vehicle
damage, the insurer may pursue the
negligent driver. Remember the trap.
Subrogation points outward toward a
responsible third party while salvage
concerns property left after a loss.
Here is a practice question in the style
of the insurance license exam.
After a covered total loss, what does
salvage mean and who may control it
after settlement? Choose the best answer
from A through D. Read every word
carefully, especially the phrase subject
to policy and law.
Pause the video and try this one before
I show the answer.
The correct answer is B.
Salvage is the damaged property that
remains after a covered loss, such as a
vehicle or building materials with
residual value. When the settlement
includes transfer of the salvage, the
insurer may take control or ownership
and arrange its preservation or
disposal.
That control is still governed by the
policy, the settlement, and applicable
law. Option A confuses salvage with the
responsible third party, which is a
subrogation issue.
Option C describes subrogation, not
remaining property.
Option D is too absolute because salvage
is not automatically abandoned and may
have value.
A subrogation analysis usually starts
with four building blocks. First, there
must be a loss covered by the policy.
Second, the insurer must have paid or
otherwise become obligated to pay the
covered claim under the applicable rule.
Third, a separate person or organization
must be legally responsible for causing
the damage.
Fourth, the recovery right must still be
enforceable.
That last element matters because a
release, waiver, limitation, or
settlement may affect what can be
recovered. The adjuster should preserve
evidence, identify the potential
tortfeasor, and avoid giving up rights
accidentally.
Consider a fire claim caused by a
negligent contractor. If the insurer
pays the covered fire damage and can
prove the contractor's negligence, the
insurer may pursue recovery. But simply
suspecting negligence is not enough.
The file must support both
responsibility and the insurer's legal
right to recover.
Subrogation has important limits that
frequently appear on exams.
The first is that an insurer generally
cannot pursue its own insured for the
covered loss through subrogation. The
purpose is to shift responsibility to an
outside wrongdoer, not to turn the
policy against the policyholder.
The second limit is no double recovery
for the same damage.
Payments from the insurer, the
responsible party, and other sources
must be coordinated. A release is
another major issue.
If the claimant releases the negligent
party before the insurer's rights are
protected, the release may prejudice or
eliminate the insurer's recovery.
That is why an adjuster should not waive
rights or settle beyond authority.
Recovery allocation can involve the
insurer's payment, the claimant's
deductible, expenses, and applicable
state law.
The exam trap is assuming the insurer
always gets every recovery dollar
automatically. Rights and allocation
depend on the facts, the agreement, and
governing law.
Workers' compensation subrogation
follows the same basic recovery idea,
but state statutes often control the
details.
An employee may receive workers'
compensation benefits for a job-related
injury without proving that the employer
was negligent. If a separate third party
caused the injury, the employer or
workers' compensation carrier may seek
recovery from that party.
A common example is an employee injured
in a crash caused by another driver. The
carrier may pay medical benefits and
wage-related benefits, then pursue the
negligent driver or that driver's
liability insurer.
The recovery may be described as
reimbursement, a lien, or a statutory
right, depending on the state. The
injured employee may also have a role in
the third-party action.
Notice, attorney fees, allocation, and
the employee's share vary by state. For
exam purposes, separate the workers'
compensation benefit obligation from the
third-party recovery right. Do not
assume the employer must have caused the
injury before subrogation can exist.
Insurance fraud is more than an error on
a claim form. It generally involves
intentional conduct designed to obtain
an insurance benefit improperly.
The conduct may be a material
misrepresentation, meaning an important
false statement. It may be concealment,
meaning knowingly hiding a relevant
fact. It may also be an intentionally
false claim, such as staging damage or
inflating an inventory. Materiality
matters because a minor, harmless
mistake is not the same as a fact that
changes coverage, value, eligibility, or
payment.
Intent matters, too. An honest
misunderstanding, memory error, or
clerical mistake is not
fraud. Adjusters should verify facts,
preserve documents, compare records, and
document inconsistencies carefully.
A red flag can justify further
investigation, but suspicion is not
proof. For example, submitting the same
stolen property loss to two insurers to
obtain duplicate benefits suggests
intentional fraud.
The ethical response is objective
investigation, not an unsupported
accusation.
A suspicious claim is not automatically
a fraudulent claim.
Fraud generally requires intentional
conduct, such as a material
misrepresentation, concealment, or
knowingly false claim for an insurance
benefit. Start by verifying the
important facts against reliable
records, policy information,
photographs, estimates, and receipts.
Preserve evidence early because
documents, digital files, or damaged
property can change or disappear. When
you find a mismatch, document exactly
what conflicts, where the information
came from, and what follow-up is needed.
Then give the claimant a fair
opportunity to explain the
inconsistency. An innocent mistake,
misunderstanding, or incomplete record
may explain a warning sign.
The adjuster must remain neutral while
separating coverage investigation,
damage measurement, and fraud review.
For example, a receipt that conflicts
with photographs calls for preservation,
questions, and comparison, not an
immediate accusation.
The exam trap is confusing suspicion
with proof. So remember that red flags
are leads that require objective
investigation.
Which statement best distinguishes
subrogation from assignment,
contribution, indemnity, and salvage?
Choose the answer that correctly
identifies the insurer's recovery right
after paying a covered loss. Pause the
video and try this one before I show the
answer.
Option A is correct because subrogation
lets an insurer pursue a responsible
third party after the insurer has paid a
covered loss.
Assignment is different because it
transfers a contractual right from one
party to another. Contribution concerns
sharing responsibility among insurers
that cover the same risk, while
indemnity describes compensation for a
covered loss rather than the recovery
right itself.
Salvage concerns damaged property or its
remaining value, not a third party's
liability. The common trap is choosing a
broad phrase about restoring the insured
because that describes indemnity more
closely than subrogation.
On the exam, look for the sequence of
insurer payment followed by recovery
against the responsible third party.
Now we move from recovery rights to the
conduct that governs every claim.
Ethics affects how an adjuster
investigates, communicates, documents,
and uses authority.
Fair treatment matters even when a
catastrophe creates pressure or a claim
appears suspicious. The next concepts
focus on honesty, conflicts, privacy,
and responsible professional judgment.
These duties apply throughout the claim,
not only when a payment decision is
made.
Ethics is the standard for how an
adjuster uses professional judgment.
Honesty means describing facts, policy
terms, authority, and decisions
accurately even when the message is
difficult. Competence means
understanding the coverage and
investigation task and seeking guidance
when an issue exceeds your knowledge.
Impartiality does not mean ignoring the
insurer's interests. It means evaluating
the claim fairly rather than favoring
either side improperly. Accurate records
should show the facts considered,
contacts made, estimates reviewed, and
reasoning behind the decision.
Confidentiality also matters because
claim files contain personal and
financial information. An adjuster must
follow licensing requirements, employer
instructions, and delegated authority.
Never promise a payment, waive a
requirement, or settle beyond the
authority granted. If an unfamiliar
coverage issue arises, the ethical
response is to obtain authorized
guidance, document the analysis, and
communicate honestly.
The exam trap is thinking loyalty to the
insurer permits misleading statements or
a biased investigation. It does not.
A conflict of interest exists when a
personal or financial connection could
affect or appear to affect claim
handling.
The connection might involve a family
member, a business interest, a vendor,
or a claimant. First, recognize the
relationship instead of assuming you can
remain objective without safeguards.
Then disclose it promptly to the
appropriate supervisor or other
authorized decision maker.
Do not accept gifts, favors, referrals,
or pressure that could influence your
judgment. Disclosure is important, but
it may not be enough by itself.
If impartiality cannot be protected, the
claim may need reassignment or another
approved safeguard.
For example, an ownership interest in a
repair vendor should be disclosed before
that vendor's invoice is evaluated. The
adjuster must not let personal gain
control coverage, damage measurement, or
settlement.
On the exam, choose the response that
protects impartiality rather than the
response that merely hides or minimizes
the connection.
Claim files often contain sensitive
personal, medical, financial, and
property information.
Confidentiality means using that
information only for a legitimate
insurance purpose connected with the
assigned work. Access should be limited
to what the adjuster needs, not
everything the system technically
permits.
Records must be protected from
unauthorized viewing, copying,
disclosure, or casual conversation.
Information may be shared with
authorized parties when it is needed for
claim handling or another legitimate
purpose.
The adjuster should also follow
applicable privacy rules, company
procedures, and state requirements. A
medical record, for example, should go
only to authorized claim participants

Salvage and subrogation both reduce an

Salvage is the damaged property left

After settlement, ownership, possession,

The insurer may control and sell the

Think of salvage as property and

The deductible must be handled before
